'''Prospect Park''' is a {{convert|526|acre|km2|adj=on}} [[urban park]] in the [[Boroughs of New York City|New York City borough]] of [[Brooklyn]]. The park is situated between the neighborhoods of [[Park Slope]], [[Prospect Heights, Brooklyn|Prospect Heights]], [[Crown Heights]], [[Prospect Lefferts Gardens]], [[Flatbush]], and [[Windsor Terrace, Brooklyn|Windsor Terrace]], and is adjacent to the [[Brooklyn Museum]], [[Grand Army Plaza]], and the [[Brooklyn Botanic Garden]].  Prospect Park is the second-largest public park in Brooklyn, behind [[Marine Park (Brooklyn park)|Marine Park]]. Designated as a [[New York City scenic landmark]] and listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]], Prospect Park is operated by the Prospect Park Alliance and NYC Parks.

First proposed in legislation passed in 1859, Prospect Park was laid out by landscape architects [[Frederick Law Olmsted]] and [[Calvert Vaux]] for the then-independent city of Brooklyn. Prospect Park opened in 1867, though it was not substantially complete until 1873. The park subsequently underwent numerous modifications and expansions to its facilities. Several additions to the park were completed in the 1890s, in the [[City Beautiful movement|City Beautiful]] architectural movement. In the early 20th century, [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] (NYC Parks) commissioner [[Robert Moses]] started a program to clean up Prospect Park. A period of decline in the late 20th century spurred the creation of the Prospect Park Alliance, which refurbished many parts of the park from the 1980s through the 2020s.

Main attractions of the park include the {{convert|90|acre|ha|adj=on}} Long Meadow; the Picnic House; [[Litchfield Villa]]; [[Prospect Park Zoo]]; the [[Boathouse on the Lullwater of the Lake in Prospect Park|Boathouse]]; [[Concert Grove]]; Brooklyn's only lake, covering {{convert|60|acre|ha|abbr=on}}; and the Prospect Park Bandshell that hosts outdoor concerts in the summertime. The park also has sports facilities, including the Prospect Park Tennis Center, basketball courts, baseball fields, soccer fields, and the New York [[Pétanque]] Club in the Parade Ground. There is also a private [[Quakers|Society of Friends]] (Quaker) cemetery on Quaker Hill near the ball fields. In addition, Prospect Park is part of the [[Brooklyn-Queens Greenway]], a network of green spaces that stretch across western [[Long Island]].

==History==
===Before the park===
[[File:Battle-Pass-1792.jpg|thumb|left|Etching of the [[Battle Pass (Brooklyn)|Battle Pass]] area from the 1776 [[Battle of Brooklyn]] in the [[American Revolutionary War]] (1775–1783). c. 1792]]

Approximately 17,000 years ago, the [[terminal moraine]] of the receding [[Last glacial period#Wisconsin glaciation, in North America|Wisconsin Glacier]] that formed [[Long Island]], known as the [[Harbor Hill Moraine]], established a string of hills and [[Kettle (landform)|kettles]] in the northern part of the park and a lower lying [[outwash plain]] in the southern part.<ref name="nycsign">{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/sub_your_park/historical_signs/hs_historical_sign.php?id=11760|title=Prospect Park: Wetlands of New York City|date=December 7, 2001|access-date=November 20, 2007|publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]|archive-date=March 12, 2005|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050312132325/http://www.nycgovparks.org/sub_your_park/historical_signs/hs_historical_sign.php?id=11760|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="USGS62">{{cite web|url=https://3dparks.wr.usgs.gov/nyc/parks/loc62.htm|title=NYC Regional Geology: 62 Prospect Park|year=2004|access-date=November 20, 2007|publisher=United States Geological Survey|archive-date=November 9, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071109174955/http://3dparks.wr.usgs.gov/nyc/parks/loc62.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> Mount Prospect (or Prospect Hill), near the intersection of [[Flatbush Avenue]] and [[Eastern Parkway]], is the highest among a string of hills that extends into the park, including Sullivan, Breeze, and Lookout. Rising 200 feet (61 m) above sea level, it is one of the tallest hills in Brooklyn.<ref name="Tate 2015 p. 220">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8xPwBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA220|title=Great City Parks|last=Tate|first=Alan|publisher=Taylor & Francis|year=2015|isbn=978-1-317-61298-8|access-date=January 29, 2019|archive-date=August 2, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230802002742/https://books.google.com/books?id=8xPwBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA220|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|218}}<ref name="USGS">{{cite map|publisher=[[United States Geological Survey|USGS]]|title=Brooklyn (NY) Topographical Map|url=https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/Maps/USTopo/PDF/NY/NY_Brooklyn_20130328_TM_geo.pdf|date=2013|access-date=January 19, 2019|archive-date=July 27, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190727033440/https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/Maps/USTopo/PDF/NY/NY_Brooklyn_20130328_TM_geo.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> The area was originally forested, but became open pasture after two centuries of European colonization. Significant stands of trees remained only in the [[Bog|peat bogs]] centered south of Ninth and Flatbush Avenues, as well as in a large bog north of Ninth Street, and contained [[chestnut]], [[Populus alba|white poplar]], and [[oak]].{{refn|name=PParkGeology|The large peat bog north of Ninth Street, running east of Prospect Park West, was called the Pigeon Ground and occupied much of the area that was to become the Long Meadow.<ref>{{cite book|last=Levison|first=Wallace Goold|editor=Louis Pope Gratacap|title="The Peat Beds of Prospect Park, Brooklyn, New York" in ''Geology of the City of New York''|publisher=H. Holt and Company|year=1909|location=New York|pages=224–225|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Klk-AAAAIAAJ&q=Brooklyn++%22Prospect+Park%22&pg=PA223|access-date=October 19, 2020|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041309/https://books.google.com/books?id=Klk-AAAAIAAJ&q=Brooklyn++%22Prospect+Park%22&pg=PA223#v=snippet&q=Brooklyn%20%20%22Prospect%20Park%22&f=false|url-status=live}}</ref>}} Some of these stands were preserved in the modern-day Prospect Park Ravine and nicknamed "The Last Forest of Brooklyn".<ref name="LastForest">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/04/09/nyregion/urban-backyard-to-be-revitalized.html|date=April 9, 1995|title=Urban Backyard To Be Revitalized|last=Martin|first=Douglas|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|work=The New York Times|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=August 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190821003147/https://www.nytimes.com/1995/04/09/nyregion/urban-backyard-to-be-revitalized.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

During the [[American Revolutionary War]] (1775–1783), the park was a site of the [[Battle of Long Island]] (aka Battle of Brooklyn). The [[Continental Army]] attempted to hold [[Battle Pass (Brooklyn)|Battle Pass]], an opening in the terminal moraine where the old Flatbush Road passed from the villages of Brooklyn to [[Flatbush]], where a large white oak tree was cut down to block the progress of the British forces.<ref>[https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/393 Dongan Oak Marker] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190703052809/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/393 |date=July 3, 2019 }}, [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]. Accessed January 1, 2024. "One of several small monuments in the vicinity of what is known as the "Battle Pass" in Prospect Park, the Dongan Oak Monument commemorates events which took place in this area during the Battle of Long Island on August 27, 1776. During this significant battle of the Revolutionary War, a large white oak mentioned in 1685 in the patent of Governor Thomas Dongan (1634–1715), was cut down by Colonial soldiers and thrown across the road to impede the advance of the British army."</ref> The pass fell after some of the heaviest fighting in the engagement, and its loss contributed to [[George Washington]]'s decision to retreat. Even though American forces lost the battle, they were able to hold the British back long enough for Washington's army to escape across the [[East River]] to [[Manhattan]]. Plaques north of the zoo, as well as the Maryland Monument at Lookout Hill's foot, honor this event.<ref name="timeline">{{cite web|url=http://www.prospectpark.org/visit/history/timeline|title=History timeline|website=prospectpark.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081231075355/http://www.prospectpark.org/visit/history/timeline|archive-date=December 31, 2008|url-status=dead|access-date=March 20, 2018}}</ref><ref name="am New York 2014">{{cite web|url=https://www.amny.com/secrets-of-new-york/secrets-of-prospect-park-1.9498571|title=Secrets of Prospect Park|date=October 19, 2014|website=am New York|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209124156/https://www.amny.com/secrets-of-new-york/secrets-of-prospect-park-1.9498571|url-status=live}}</ref>

The then-independent city of Brooklyn built [[Ridgewood Reservoir]] on Prospect Hill in 1856 to serve its western half.<ref>{{cite web|last=Spellen|first=Suzanne|title=Past and Present: The Mt. Prospect Reservoir|website=Brownstoner|date=July 22, 2011|url=https://www.brownstoner.com/history/past-and-present-the-mt-prospect-reservoir/|access-date=July 5, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240101173823/https://www.brownstoner.com/history/past-and-present-the-mt-prospect-reservoir/|archive-date=January 1, 2024|quote=In 1856, the city of Brooklyn built a huge reservoir on the top of the hill to supply water to the western part of the city. The water came from the Ridgewood Reservoir in Cypress Hills, flowing to Mt. Prospect through underground pipes. The 80' tower at the edge of the reservoir also held water, which then flowed to a pumping station on Underhill Avenue, and then on down the line to homes and businesses.|url-status=live}}</ref> The need to keep the lots around the reservoir free of development, as well as the preservation of the Battle Pass area, were cited as two reasons for establishing a large park nearby.<ref name="Lancaster">{{cite book|url=https://www.echonyc.com/~parks/books/handbook.html|title=Prospect Park Handbook|last=Lancaster|first=Clay|publisher=Long Island University Press|year=1972|isbn=978-0-913252-06-2|edition=2nd|location=New York|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=October 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191001181824/https://www.echonyc.com/~parks/books/handbook.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Planning===
[[File:Frederick Law Olmsted.jpg|thumb|upright| Landscape architect [[Frederick Law Olmsted]], as depicted by [[John Singer Sargent]] in 1895]]
The original impetus to build Prospect Park stemmed from an April 18, 1859, act of the New York State Legislature, empowering a twelve-member commission to recommend sites for parks in the [[City of Brooklyn]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BBYZAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA1|title=Laws Relating to the Public Parks, Parkways, and Other Property Under the Care and Control of the Brooklyn Park Commissioners|last=Anderson|first=J.A.|year=1887|page=1|access-date=January 20, 2019|archive-date=August 1, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230801235750/https://books.google.com/books?id=BBYZAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA1|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Brooklyn Daily Eagle 1860">{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/3137046/|title=Public Parks and Promenades|date=May 29, 1860|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=January 19, 2019|page=2|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=August 1, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230801235739/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/article/3137046/|url-status=live}}</ref> At the time, Brooklyn was promoted as New York City's first [[commuter suburb]],<ref>Margino, Megan. [https://www.nypl.org/blog/2016/05/10/history-nyc-commuter "From Suburb to City and Back Again: A Brief History of the NYC Commuter"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041311/https://www.nypl.org/blog/2016/05/10/history-nyc-commuter |date=January 24, 2024 }}, [[New York Public Library]], May 10, 2016. Accessed January 1, 2024.</ref> and it became the third largest city in the country from 1860 to 1880, behind New York City (which then included [[Manhattan]] and parts of [[the Bronx]]) and [[Philadelphia]].<ref>Berman, Andrew (August 9, 2016). [https://gothamist.com/news/sorry-chicago-brooklyn-will-soon-be-the-third-largest-city-in-america "Sorry, Chicago: Brooklyn Will Soon Be The Third Largest City In America"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240101173824/https://gothamist.com/news/sorry-chicago-brooklyn-will-soon-be-the-third-largest-city-in-america |date=January 1, 2024 }}, ''[[Gothamist]]'', August 9, 2016. Accessed January 1, 2024. "Brooklyn has held the Third City spot twice before: From 1860–1880, when Philly was No. 2 and New York, which comprised Manhattan and parts of today's Bronx, was No. 1; and again (unofficially) from 1910, when it overtook Philadelphia, until 1970, when the population of Los Angeles surpassed Brooklyn's for the first time."</ref> During this time, concepts concerning public parks gained popularity. In 1858, [[landscape architects]] [[Frederick Law Olmsted]] and [[Calvert Vaux]] had created the design for [[Central Park]] in Manhattan, which became the first landscaped park in the United States.<ref name="timeline" /><ref name="Lancaster" /> [[James S. T. Stranahan]], then President of the Brooklyn Board of Park Commissioners, believed that a park in Brooklyn "would become a favorite resort for all classes of our community, enabling thousands to enjoy pure air, with healthful exercise, at all seasons of the year..." He also thought a public park would attract wealthy residents.<ref name="timeline" /> Stranahan originally envisioned one large park extending eastward to 
the community of [[Jamaica, Queens|Jamaica]] and what was then [[Queens|Queens County]]. However, the city's rapid development made this impossible, and today, the largest remnants of this proposed landscape are Prospect Park and the {{Convert|538|acre|ha|abbr=|adj=on}} [[Forest Park (Queens)|Forest Park]] in Queens.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://qns.com/story/2018/09/08/oak-ridge-house-forest-park-rich-queens-history-neighborhood-way/|title=Oak Ridge house in Forest Park is rich in Queens history: Our Neighborhood, The Way it Was|website=QNS.com|author=Woodhaven Cultural and Historical Society|date=September 8, 2018 |language=en-US|access-date=May 31, 2019|archive-date=July 26, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190726085449/https://qns.com/story/2018/09/08/oak-ridge-house-forest-park-rich-queens-history-neighborhood-way/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In February 1860, a group of fifteen commissioners submitted suggestions for locations of four large parks and three small parks in Brooklyn, as well as a series of boulevards to connect them.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Brooklyn Daily Eagle 1860" /><ref name="Bluestone 1987">{{cite journal|last=Bluestone|first=Daniel M.|year=1987|title=From Promenade to Park: The Gregarious Origins of Brooklyn's Park Movement|journal=American Quarterly|publisher=JSTOR|volume=39|issue=4|pages=529–550|doi=10.2307/2713123|issn=0003-0678|jstor=2713123}}</ref> The largest of these proposed parks was a {{convert|320|acre|km2|adj=on}} plot centered on Mount Prospect and bounded by Warren Street to the north; Vanderbilt, Ninth, and Tenth Avenues to the west; Third and Ninth Streets to the south; and Washington Avenue to the east.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/27409545/|title=Prospect Park|date=May 19, 1861|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=January 19, 2019|page=2|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=August 1, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230801235739/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/article/27409545/|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Egbert Viele]] began drawing plans for "Mount Prospect Park", as the space was initially called, and published his proposal in 1861. The park was to straddle Flatbush Avenue and include Prospect Hill, as well as the land now occupied by the [[Central Library (Brooklyn Public Library)|Brooklyn Public Library]], [[Brooklyn Botanic Garden]], and [[Brooklyn Museum]].<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Bluestone 1987" />

By late 1860, land had been purchased for Viele's plan.<ref name="Lancaster" /> However, the onset of the [[American Civil War|Civil War]] stopped further activity, and the boulevards and smaller parks were pushed back.<ref name="Bluestone 1987" /> The delay prompted some reflection; Stranahan invited Calvert Vaux to review Viele's plans early in 1865.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="PPAHistory">{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/learn-more/park-history-slideshow/|title=History and Nature: History of the Park|year=2007|publisher=Prospect Park Alliance|access-date=November 23, 2007|archive-date=December 24, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141224055718/http://prospectpark.org/learn-more/park-history-slideshow/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Vaux took issue with Flatbush Avenue's division of the park, thought that the park should have a lake, and urged for southward expansion beyond the city limits and into the then-independent town of [[Flatbush, Brooklyn|Flatbush]].<ref name="PPGuide">
{{cite book|title=The Complete Illustrated Guidebook to Prospect Park and the Brooklyn Botanic Garden|last=Berenson|first=Richard J.|author2=deMause, Neil|publisher=Silver Lining Books|year=2001|isbn=978-0-7607-2213-8|location=New York|author-link2=Neil deMause}}
</ref>{{Rp|86–91}} Vaux's February 1865 proposal reflected the present layout of the park: three distinctive regions, meadow in the north and west, a wooded ravine in the east, and a lake in the south, without being divided by Flatbush Avenue. Vaux included an oval plaza at the northern end of the park, which would later become [[Grand Army Plaza]].<ref>[https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B040/history Grand Army Plaza] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207015324/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B040/history |date=February 7, 2019 }}, [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]. Accessed January 1, 2024. "Grand Army Plaza, the oval at the main entrance of Brooklyn's Prospect Park, was meant to provide a wide and picturesque approach to the park, which park designer Calvert Vaux (1824–1895) considered a vital design element. The Plaza was one of the first features of Prospect Park to be built and marks the beginning of the Eastern Parkway (1866), the world's first parkway, also designed by Vaux and his partner Frederick Law Olmsted (1822–1903)."</ref><ref>[https://www.tclf.org/landscapes/grand-army-plaza-brooklyn Grand Army Plaza – Brooklyn] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240108031319/https://www.tclf.org/landscapes/grand-army-plaza-brooklyn |date=January 8, 2024 }}, [[The Cultural Landscape Foundation]]. Accessed January 1, 2024. "First envisioned in 1865, the plaza was conceived as the primary entrance for Olmsted and Vaux's 526-acre Prospect Park. The elliptical plaza capped the park's northern tip with a paved, pedestrian area ringed by carriageways and heavily-planted crescent-shaped berms."</ref> The revised plan called for the purchase of additional parcels to the south and west to accommodate Prospect Lake, but it excluded parcels already purchased east of Flatbush Avenue, including Prospect Hill itself. In addition, engineer-in-charge Joseph P. Davis and assistants John Bogart and John Y. Culyer were named to work on the project.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="The New York Times 1868">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1868/12/15/archives/prospect-park-progress-of-the-workdescriptive-particulars.html|title=Prospect Park; Progress of the Work—Descriptive Particulars.|date=December 15, 1868|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 28, 2019|archive-date=January 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129064330/https://www.nytimes.com/1868/12/15/archives/prospect-park-progress-of-the-workdescriptive-particulars.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/stream/annualreportsofb1873broo/annualreportsofb1873broo_djvu.txt|title=Annual reports of the Brooklyn Park Commissioners, 1861–1873|date=1873|publisher=Brooklyn Park Commissioners|page=127|access-date=January 28, 2019|via=Internet Archive}}</ref>[[File:Friends Cemetery road PPW jeh.jpg|thumb|Friends Cemetery]]

By then, land speculation was underway. The plot bounded by Ninth and Tenth Avenues between Third and Fifteenth Streets was held by real estate developer Edwin Clarke Litchfield, who had erected his home, [[Litchfield Villa|Litchfield Manor]], on the east side of Ninth Avenue in 1857.<ref name="Litchfield">{{cite web|title=Litchfield Villa|work=Prospect Park Alliance: Official WebSite of Prospect Park|publisher=Prospect Park Alliance|year=2008|url=http://www.prospectpark.org/history_nature/historic_places/h_villa|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081029064752/http://www.prospectpark.org/history_nature/historic_places/h_villa|archive-date=October 29, 2008}}</ref> The Parks Commission ultimately acquired the Litchfield plot in 1868 for $1.7 million, forty-two percent of the overall expenditure for land, even though the plot constituted just over five percent of the park's acreage. Much of this acreage houses the maintenance yards and is rarely seen by the public.<ref name="ArchGuide">{{cite book|last=Morrone|first=Francis|title=An Architectural Guidebook to Brooklyn|publisher=Gibbs-Smith|location=Salt Lake City|year=2001|isbn=978-1-58685-047-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cIOZO8_HNGAC&pg=PP1|access-date=October 23, 2016|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041314/https://books.google.com/books?id=cIOZO8_HNGAC&pg=PP1#v=onepage&q&f=false|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1866, the New York state legislature passed a bill approving the acquisition of additional land on the southwest side of the park.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Commissioners of Prospect Park 1868">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/stream/annualreportofco18611868/annualreportofco18611868_djvu.txt|title=Annual report of the Commissioners of Prospect Park|date=1868|publisher=Commissioners of Prospect Park|page=68|access-date=January 28, 2019|via=Internet Archive}}</ref> The park was built around the preexisting Quaker cemetery,<ref name="Biederman 1998"/> which was accommodated by an agreement under which the Society of Friends deeded their unused acreage to the park. In exchange, they retained the remaining 10 acres for their private cemetery in perpetuity, as well as the rights to access the cemetery.<ref name="Lancaster" />

=== Construction ===
Despite the repercussions of Vaux's revisions, Stranahan championed the revised proposal. Vaux recruited Olmsted and formally presented the plan in February 1866.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50380116/|title=Prospect Park; The Architect's Plan For Its Improvement|date=February 5, 1866|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=January 28, 2019|page=2|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=January 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129122819/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50380116/|url-status=live}}</ref> The revised plan was accepted by May. Construction started the following month, and initial work focused on draining the land.<ref name="Lancaster" /> Then, the roads, bridle paths, and walks within Prospect Park were graded and individual features were landscaped. Three scenic roads, the West, Center, and East Drives, were built within the perimeters of the park. Depending on the time of year, between 250 and 2,000 workers were employed.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="The New York Times 1868" /><ref name="Yale University Press 2010">{{Cite enc-nyc2|page=1043}}</ref> Much of the landscaping focused on removing obstructions such as pits and swamps, and enhancing other natural features such as hills. Trees were only removed if they blocked a roadway or path that was being built.<ref name="nyc.gov 1871">{{Cite web|url=http://home2.nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/4278annual_report_brooklyn_parks_comm_1870.pdf|title=1870 Brooklyn Park Commissioners Annual Report|date=January 1871|website=[[Government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]|access-date=January 29, 2019|archive-date=February 11, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170211165858/http://home2.nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/4278annual_report_brooklyn_parks_comm_1870.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Rp|38}}

The first section of the park opened to the public on October 19, 1867, while it was still under construction. The segment that was open to the public included part of the East Drive between the north end of the park, at modern-day Grand Army Plaza, and Coney Island Avenue at the southeast corner.<ref name="Eagle">{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50505232/|title=Prospect Park|date=October 21, 1867|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|publisher=I. Van Anden|page=2|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|access-date=February 13, 2019|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214002753/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50505232/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1867/10/22/archives/prospect-park.html|title=Prospect Park.|date=October 22, 1867|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 28, 2019|archive-date=January 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129122805/https://www.nytimes.com/1867/10/22/archives/prospect-park.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The park initially contained the Playground, which had a croquet lawn, a sailboat pond, a maze, and a summer house.  By 1868, the open portions of Prospect Park were patronized by 100,000 people per month,<ref name="Lancaster" /> and several miles of roads, paths, and walkways had been completed.<ref name="The New York Times 1868" /> The land for Prospect Park's Parade Ground was acquired that year.<ref name="Commissioners of Prospect Park 1868" /> A series of pedestrian arches to separate pedestrian and vehicular traffic in the park were also built during this time.<ref name="Lancaster" />

Over 200 benches were installed to accommodate the new visitors. Rustic wooden shelters with "various oblong and polygonal shapes" were placed along the shore of Prospect Park's lake and were designed to be used as scenic overlooks. Several bridges and eight hundred bird houses were installed to enhance the park's rustic quality.<ref name="Lancaster" /> In its 1870 annual report, the Brooklyn park commissioners reported that the lake was nearly completed, and that widening of nearby streets was underway.<ref name="nyc.gov 1871" />{{Rp|9, 11}} By 1871, the monthly visitor count had increased to 250,000.<ref name="Lancaster" /> The park's patronage continued to increase, and in an 1873 article, ''The New York Times'' described Prospect Park as having become an "indispensable Sunday resort for the toiling thousands of Brooklyn."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1873/08/11/archives/prospect-park-the-view-from-the-reservoir-boating-on-the-lake-the.html|title=Prospect Park.; the View from the Reservoir Boating on the Lake. the Central Park. the Merrick Camp-Meeting. Departure of the Highlanders. the Labor Movement.|date=August 11, 1873|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209124724/https://www.nytimes.com/1873/08/11/archives/prospect-park-the-view-from-the-reservoir-boating-on-the-lake-the.html|url-status=live}}</ref> However, the high patronage also had downsides: an 1875 editorial in the ''Times'' observed that many people would take shortcuts along the grass rather than travel on designated routes.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1875/06/22/archives/prospect-park.html|title=Prospect Park.|date=June 22, 1875|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 12, 2019|archive-date=February 13, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190213011730/https://www.nytimes.com/1875/06/22/archives/prospect-park.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

Prospect Park was substantially complete in 1873, but with the [[Panic of 1873|financial panic of that year]], Olmsted and Vaux stopped collaborating on the park's construction. Some of the originally envisioned facets of the park, such as an observation tower, a terraced restaurant, and a [[Spinning top|top]]-shaped Carriage Concourse, were not built.<ref name="am New York 2014" /><ref name="Dailey 2013" /> Olmsted and Vaux had also planned for a system of parkways to connect to Prospect Park, though only two were built: [[Ocean Parkway (Brooklyn)|Ocean Parkway]], running to [[Coney Island]] in the south, and [[Eastern Parkway]], running to [[Crown Heights|Crown Heights, Brooklyn]] in the east.<ref name="Yale University Press 2010" /> Overall, the city of Brooklyn spent more than $4 million to acquire the parkland, while the actual cost of construction amounted to more than $5 million.<ref name="Lancaster" />

Stranahan was regarded by his 19th-century peers as the true "Father of Prospect Park", a reputation established through his 22-year reign as Park Commission president (1860–1882), engagement of Olmsted and Vaux, overseeing complex land acquisitions,<ref name="EagleEditorial">{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50425489/|title=The Park "Magician": Is He Cornered At Last?|date=June 7, 1882|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=November 20, 2007|publisher=Brooklyn Eagle Inc.|at=p. 2, cols. 1–2|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215050320/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50425489/|url-status=live}}</ref> securing funding to build the park, and after the park's completion, defending the park against changes that were not compatible with the overall design.<ref>{{cite news|title=Mr. Stranahan Dead|date=September 3, 1898|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|at=[https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50338959/ p. 1, col 1]; [https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50338960/ p. 2, cols 4–6] {{open access}}}}</ref> A [[statue of James S. T. Stranahan]] was proposed in 1890.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/60726980/|title=For A Statue; In Honor of James S. T. Stranahan|date=January 15, 1890|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=May 27, 2007|at=p. 6, col. 3|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215050411/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/60726980/|url-status=live}}</ref> Located inside the Grand Army Plaza entrance, the statue was sculpted by [[Frederick William MacMonnies|Frederick MacMonnies]] and presented to Stranahan in June 1891.<ref name="BrooklynEagleStranahan">{{cite news|title=The Father of the Park|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|at=p. 20, col. 3|publisher=Brooklyn Eagle Inc.|date=June 7, 1891|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50448986/|access-date=November 20, 2007|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214002737/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50448986/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Late 19th century ===
[[File:Prospect Park, Brooklyn, 1880. (5832926707).jpg|thumb|Prospect Park in 1880]]Prospect Park became widely used after its opening, and many sports were hosted there. By the late 19th century, [[archery]] was among the most popular sports being practiced on the Long Meadow,<ref name="Dailey 2013" /> and up to 100 groups would convene on the Long Meadow to play [[croquet]] on weekend afternoons.<ref name="The New York Times 2014">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/07/08/nyregion/a-brief-history-of-croquet-in-brooklyn.html|url-access=subscription|first1=Emily S.|last1=Rueb|title=A Flashback to Croquet's Heyday in Prospect Park|date=July 8, 2014|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216035428/https://www.nytimes.com/2014/07/08/nyregion/a-brief-history-of-croquet-in-brooklyn.html|url-status=live}}</ref> During winters, people practiced "ice baseball" on the lake.<ref name="Dailey 2013">{{cite web|url=https://ny.curbed.com/2013/8/7/10210902/25-little-known-facts-about-olmsted-vauxs-masterpiece|title=25 Little-Known Facts About Olmsted & Vaux's Masterpiece|last=Dailey|first=Jessica|date=August 7, 2013|website=Curbed NY|access-date=January 28, 2019|archive-date=January 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129010331/https://ny.curbed.com/2013/8/7/10210902/25-little-known-facts-about-olmsted-vauxs-masterpiece|url-status=dead}}</ref> Ice skating was also a common sport, and was frequently practiced on the lake during the winter.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1893/01/25/archives/skating-at-prospect-park-women-who-can-do-tricks-on-skates-like-the.html|url-access=subscription|title=Skating at Prospect Park.; Women Who Can Do Tricks on Skates Like the Men.|date=January 25, 1893|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215051002/https://www.nytimes.com/1893/01/25/archives/skating-at-prospect-park-women-who-can-do-tricks-on-skates-like-the.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Because picnicking was banned in Central Park, and generally disapproved-of in many other parks in Manhattan, Prospect Park became a popular picnic spot.<ref name="am New York 2014" /><ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50333245/|title=Prospect Park Picnics|date=August 15, 1886|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=January 28, 2019|page=11|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=January 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129064017/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50333245/|url-status=live}}</ref> However, this also resulted in litter, and by 1881, ''The New York Times'' was receiving complaints about a lack of cleanliness in the park.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1881/06/03/archives/facts-about-prospect-park-the-great-pleasure-ground-not-quite-gone.html|title=Facts About Prospect Park.; the Great Pleasure Ground Not Quite Gone to Decay.|date=June 3, 1881|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215050855/https://www.nytimes.com/1881/06/03/archives/facts-about-prospect-park-the-great-pleasure-ground-not-quite-gone.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

No new structures were constructed in Prospect Park until 1882, when a utilitarian brick stable was constructed on the park's western side.<ref name="Lancaster" /> The same year, Brooklyn mayor [[Seth Low]] did not reappoint Stranahan or the other commissioners, a change that neither Stranahan nor the other commissioners actively opposed. Stranahan, for his part, was becoming more engaged in other Brooklyn concerns.<ref name="Low">{{cite news|title=Municipal: Interesting Happenings at City Hall Today|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|at=p. 4, col. 3|publisher=Brooklyn Eagle Inc.|date=June 7, 1882|url=http://eagle.brooklynpubliclibrary.org/Default/Layout/Includes/BE/ArtWin.asp?From=Search&Key=BEG%2F1882%2F06%2F15%2F4%2FAr00400%2Exml&CollName=BEG%5FCOL2&DOCID=2050299&Keyword=%28%3Cmany%3E%3Cstem%3EStranahan%29&skin=BE&AppName=2&ViewMode=GIF <!--https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50425491/-->|access-date=November 23, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080103060805/http://eagle.brooklynpubliclibrary.org/Default/Layout/Includes/BE/ArtWin.asp?From=Search&Key=BEG%2F1882%2F06%2F15%2F4%2FAr00400%2Exml&CollName=BEG%5FCOL2&DOCID=2050299&Keyword=%28%3Cmany%3E%3Cstem%3EStranahan%29&skin=BE&AppName=2&ViewMode=GIF|archive-date=January 3, 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> The action, however, did signal a change in the style of park management, which grew to embrace neoclassicism.<ref name="PPAHistory" />

Simultaneously during the 1880s, the quality of Prospect Park had declined through overuse and a corresponding lack of maintenance.<ref name="Dailey 2013" /> After Brooklyn Mayor [[Alfred C. Chapin]] walked through the park in 1888, he requested that $100,000 be allocated for improvements.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1888/04/20/archives/prospect-parks-decay-mayor-chapin-wants-100000-appropriated-at-once.html|title=Prospect Park's Decay.; Mayor Chapin Wants $100,000 Appropriated at Once.|date=April 20, 1888|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215051011/https://www.nytimes.com/1888/04/20/archives/prospect-parks-decay-mayor-chapin-wants-100000-appropriated-at-once.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Subsequently, the Brooklyn Parks Commission embarked on a $200,000 program to restore the park. It repaved many of the walkways and drives, as well as replanted flora.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://home2.nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/3962annual_report_brooklyn_dept_parks_1889.pdf|title=1889 Brooklyn Borough Parks Department Annual Report|date=January 7, 1890|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=May 29, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100529112838/http://home2.nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/3962annual_report_brooklyn_dept_parks_1889.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Rp|9–12}} Ornate gateways were added to the Ocean Parkway and Willink Plaza entrances.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1888-10-17|title=Park Improvements|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-brooklyn-citizen-park-improvements/151128734/|access-date=2024-07-11|work=The Brooklyn Citizen|pages=6}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=1888-12-12|title=Contractors Indignant|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-union-contractors-indignant/151128685/|access-date=2024-07-11|work=Times Union|pages=1}}</ref> The commission also proposed purchasing the land around the Mount Prospect Reservoir, northeast of modern-day Prospect Park, which had been excluded from the final plan for the park.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://home2.nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/3960annual_report_brooklyn_dept_parks_1888.pdf|title=1888 Brooklyn Borough Parks Department Annual Report|date=March 11, 1889|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 3, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170203140155/http://home2.nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/3960annual_report_brooklyn_dept_parks_1888.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Rp|54–64}}<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50455430/|title=For Public Use: Proposing to Retain the East Side Lands|date=April 3, 1889|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=February 14, 2019|page=3|via=Newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215050529/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50455430/|url-status=live}}</ref> Instead, this space was developed as the [[Brooklyn Museum]] in the 1890s, followed by the [[Central Library (Brooklyn Public Library)|Brooklyn Central Library]] and [[Brooklyn Botanic Garden]] in the early 20th century.<ref name="Lancaster" /> The reservoir was filled in, and along with Mount Prospect Hill, became the separate [[Mount Prospect Park]] in 1940.<ref name="Kadinsky20162" />

The park and its surroundings were subsequently restored in the 1890s during the [[City Beautiful movement]].<ref name="Dailey 2013" /> After the Soldier's and Sailor's Arch at Grand Army Plaza was built in 1892, the park commissioners engaged the [[McKim, Mead, and White]] architectural firm to redesign Grand Army Plaza in a complementary, neoclassical way. By 1896, Grand Army Plaza sported [[:File:Prospect Park Entrance From Memorial Arch.jpg|four towering granite columns]] adorned with carved [[wikt:fasces|fasces]] and eagles at the base, though the bronze eagles atop the columns would not be installed until 1902. Granite fencing with decorative bronze urns replaced simple wooden fencing, and polygonal granite pavilions on the east and west corners of the park supplanted earlier rustic shelters. All the major entrances of the park gained similar neoclassical treatments. By the turn of the twentieth century, sculptures by [[Frederick MacMonnies]] graced the Arch and works by MacMonnies and [[Alexander Phimister Proctor|Alexander Proctor]] adorned many of the entrances.<ref name="PPAHistory" />

Neoclassical structures appeared elsewhere within the park. McKim, Mead and White designed the Ocean Parkway and Willink entrances, which opened in 1890.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1890-08-03|title=New Park Entrances|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-brooklyn-daily-eagle-new-prospect-pa/14753745/|access-date=2024-07-11|work=The Brooklyn Daily Eagle|pages=3}}</ref> The same firm transformed the Children's Playground and Pools in the park's northeast quadrant into the Rose Garden and the Vale of Cashmere, each a formally arranged space, in 1893–1894.<ref name="Lancaster" />  [[Stanford White]]'s Maryland Monument was installed near the Terrace Bridge in 1895 in recognition of the [[Maryland 400]], who fought in the Battle of Long Island on the slopes of Lookout Hill.<ref name="Tate 2015 p. 220" />{{Rp|130}}<ref name="PPAArch">{{cite web|url=http://www.prospectpark.org/visit/history/architects|title=Olmsted and Vaux|year=2008|access-date=March 21, 2009|publisher=Prospect Park Alliance|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090322230433/http://www.prospectpark.org/visit/history/architects|archive-date=March 22, 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref><gallery heights="150" widths="150" class="center">

=== Early 20th century ===
[[File:ProspectPark 1901Plan.jpg|thumb|left|1901 map of Prospect Park, published in the Parks Department's 1902 Annual Report]]

The city of Brooklyn merged with Manhattan and other outlying boroughs in 1898, creating the City of Greater New York. By the end of the century, Prospect Park saw about 15 million visitors per year.<ref name="Yale University Press 2010" /> Though people were officially banned from hosting picnics and other large eating events in Prospect Park, the rule was not enforced for several years until 1903, when a surge of visitors from Manhattan led to an increase in luncheons being hosted.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1903/07/21/archives/no-eating-in-prospect-park-manhattan-visitors-too-careless-with.html|title=No Eating in Prospect Park; Manhattan Visitors Too Careless with Refuse Led to Blue Laws.|date=July 21, 1903|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215051011/https://www.nytimes.com/1903/07/21/archives/no-eating-in-prospect-park-manhattan-visitors-too-careless-with.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1907, lights were installed to deter couples from kissing or other intimate activity within the park.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/1736457/|title=Kennedy and Cozier Conspire Against Cupid|date=July 12, 1907|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=February 14, 2019|page=2|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041208/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/article/the-brooklyn-daily-eagle/1736457/|url-status=live}}</ref> At the same time, the city embarked on an improvement program at Prospect Park by cleaning out the landscape, constructing the [[Bartel-Pritchard Square]] entrance, and removing an old boathouse that had been supplanted by the Boathouse on the Lullwater.<ref>{{Cite news|title=PRIMING UP CITY'S PARKS: Many Changes Are Now Under Way in Prospect Park|date=April 26, 1908|work=New-York Tribune|page=C8|id={{ProQuest|572080805}}}}</ref>

The construction of structures continued in the first decade of the 20th century. The neoclassical [[Grecian Shelter|Peristyle]] (1904), [[Boathouse on the Lullwater of the Lake in Prospect Park|Boathouse]] (1905), Tennis House (1910), and [[Willink Plaza|Willink Comfort Station]] (1912) were all designed by Helmle, Hudswell and Huberty, alumni and proteges of McKim, Mead, and White.<ref name="Tate 2015 p. 220" />{{Rp|130}}<ref name="PPAArch" /> The entrances into Prospect Park that were constructed during this time were also in the neoclassical style.<ref name="Tate 2015 p. 220" />{{Rp|130}}<ref name="Lancaster" /> Two now-demolished structures were also constructed on the peninsula, the Model Yacht Club House (1900–1956) and a shelter (1915 – {{Circa|1940s}}).<ref name="Lancaster" /> Olmsted was said to have been "distressed" by these modifications to the park's original plan.<ref name="Yale University Press 2010" />

From [[World War I]] to the mayoral administration of [[Fiorello La Guardia]] in the 1930s, investment in park infrastructure declined. A two-story brick building was opened in the Menagerie in 1916, housing monkeys, some small mammals, and several birds.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1916/04/30/archives/open-prospect-park-zoo-new-menagerie-building-dedicated-by.html|title=Open Prospect Park Zoo; New Menagerie Building Dedicated by Commissioner Ingersoll.|date=April 30, 1916|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215102809/https://www.nytimes.com/1916/04/30/archives/open-prospect-park-zoo-new-menagerie-building-dedicated-by.html|url-status=live}}</ref> After the end of World War I, a memorial commemorating fallen soldiers was proposed;<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1919/02/20/archives/plan-soldiers-memorial-brooklyn-monument-in-prospect-park-to-bear.html|title=Plan Soldiers' Memorial; Brooklyn Monument in Prospect Park to Bear About 2,000 Names.|date=February 20, 1919|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215102817/https://www.nytimes.com/1919/02/20/archives/plan-soldiers-memorial-brooklyn-monument-in-prospect-park-to-bear.html|url-status=live}}</ref> it was dedicated in 1921.<ref name="Prospect Park Monuments 1939" /> The only other structures to be built during this period were the Picnic House (1927) and a small comfort station at the Ocean Avenue entrance (1930), both designed by J. Sarsfield Kennedy.<ref name="Lancaster" /> A golf course was proposed for the Long Meadow in the 1920s, but eventually, it was built on the Peninsula, abutting the Lake at the park's southern end.<ref name="Dailey 2013" /> In 1932, a faux [[Mount Vernon]] was built in Prospect Park to commemorate the [[wikt:bicentennial|bicentennial]] of [[George Washington]]'s birthday.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=http://nymag.com/arts/books/features/robert-sullivan-my-american-revolution-2012-9/|title=Permanent Revolution|magazine=New York magazine|date=September 10, 2012|access-date=April 7, 2014|archive-date=April 8, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140408213414/http://nymag.com/arts/books/features/robert-sullivan-my-american-revolution-2012-9/|url-status=live}}</ref> However, Prospect Park was in stasis for the most part, and like many of the city's parks, it was run year-after-year with declining budgets. ''The New York Times'' observed that by the 1930s, "generations of Parks Department officials had lived well and got rich by diverting maintenance funds, and the park showed the result of a half century of abuse and neglect."<ref name="NYTOlmstedMoses">{{cite news|title=Olmsted and Moses Were the Key Figures in Development of City Parks|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|date=October 13, 1980|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1980/10/13/archives/olmsted-and-moses-were-the-key-figures-in-development-of-city-parks.html|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=August 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190821003142/https://www.nytimes.com/1980/10/13/archives/olmsted-and-moses-were-the-key-figures-in-development-of-city-parks.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Robert Moses era===
In January 1934, newly elected Mayor Fiorello La Guardia appointed [[Robert Moses]] as the commissioner of the New York City Department of Parks (NYC Parks), a new organization that eliminated borough park commissioners.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1934/01/19/archives/smith-hails-moses-as-city-parks-head-tells-of-his-service-to-state.html|title=Smith Hails Moses As City Parks Head; Tells of His Service to State and City at Luncheon Given by Long Island Leaders|date=January 19, 1934|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 16, 2019|archive-date=February 17, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190217084910/https://www.nytimes.com/1934/01/19/archives/smith-hails-moses-as-city-parks-head-tells-of-his-service-to-state.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Moses would remain commissioner for the next twenty-six years, leaving significant impacts on the city's parks. Moses used federal monies made available to relieve [[Great Depression|Depression]]-era unemployment, and this resulted in a boom in construction at Prospect Park.<ref name="PPAHistory" /><ref name="ZooOpening" />  The [[Prospect Park Zoo]] opened in 1935 on the east side of the park, replacing the former Menagerie.<ref name="ZooOpening">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1935/07/04/archives/smith-decries-backalley-politics-of-la-guardia-in-row-with-moses-at.html|title=Smith Decries 'Back-Alley Politics' Of La Guardia in Row With Moses; At Opening of New Prospect Park Zoo Former Governor Extols Park Commissioner, Who Joins Mayor in Shunning Ceremony – 3,000 View Glittering $500,000 Centre.|date=July 4, 1935|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 16, 2019|archive-date=June 18, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180618125653/https://www.nytimes.com/1935/07/04/archives/smith-decries-backalley-politics-of-la-guardia-in-row-with-moses-at.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The Bandshell and five playgrounds were also constructed toward the end of the 1930s.<ref name="PPAHistory" /><ref name="ZooOpening"/> In addition, the Carousel was opened in 1949 as a gift from the foundation of the late philanthropist [[Michael Friedsam]].<ref name="Hanmer 1952">{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/757932/|title=Big, Small Fry Vie for Brass Ring|last=Hanmer|first=Wendell|date=October 22, 1952|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=February 14, 2019|page=3|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041209/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/article/the-brooklyn-daily-eagle/757932/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="The New York Times 1952">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1952/10/22/archives/carrousel-is-dedicated-prospect-park-merrygoround-gets-official.html|title=Carrousel is Dedicated; Prospect Park Merry-Go-Round Gets Official City Send-Off|date=October 22, 1952|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 16, 2019|archive-date=February 17, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190217030435/https://www.nytimes.com/1952/10/22/archives/carrousel-is-dedicated-prospect-park-merrygoround-gets-official.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Moses also enacted new policies at the park, including a ban on sheep grazing at the Long Meadow.<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|16}}<ref name="Jacobs 2017" />

During [[World War II]], Prospect Park hosted a portion of the city's antiaircraft defense. Three hundred soldiers manned batteries, underground ammunition dumps, observation towers, repair shops and barracks around Swan Lake in the Long Meadow. Though the defenses were disbanded in 1944, traces of slit trenches and sandbagged gun emplacements could still be found several years afterward.<ref>{{cite book|last=Willensky|first=E.|title=When Brooklyn was the World, 1920–1957|publisher=Harmony Books|year=1986|isbn=978-0-517-55858-4|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7JIMAAAAYAAJ|access-date=February 20, 2019|page=210|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041206/https://books.google.com/books?id=7JIMAAAAYAAJ|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1959, the southern third of the Long Meadow was graded and fenced off for ballfields.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Illson 1959">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1959/10/17/archives/pruning-and-cleaning-begun-in-prospect-park-city-says-program-will.html|title=Pruning and Cleaning Begun in Prospect Park; City Says Program Will Make Area Prettier and Safer Department Splits Job Into 5 Sections in 5-Year Effort|last=Illson|first=Murray|date=October 17, 1959|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209124815/https://www.nytimes.com/1959/10/17/archives/pruning-and-cleaning-begun-in-prospect-park-city-says-program-will.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Prospect Park boathouse (61446p).jpg|thumb|The Boathouse on the Lullwater, almost demolished in 1964|alt=]]

Plans for the Kate Wollman Memorial Rink were approved in 1960,<ref name="The New York Times 1960" /> and the rink opened in December 1961.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1961/12/23/archives/new-wollman-rink-is-dedicated-in-brooklyn.html|title=New Wollman Rink Is Dedicated in Brooklyn|date=December 23, 1961|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 16, 2019|archive-date=October 22, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191022031526/https://www.nytimes.com/1961/12/23/archives/new-wollman-rink-is-dedicated-in-brooklyn.html|url-status=live}}</ref>  The rink was built on a filled-in portion of Prospect Lake, necessitating the removal of Music Island and the panoramic view of the lake created by Olmsted and Vaux.<ref name="The New York Times 1960">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1960/10/07/archives/prospect-park-rink-approved-wollman-fund-gives-300000.html|title=Prospect Park Rink Approved; Wollman Fund Gives $300,000|date=October 7, 1960|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209130318/https://www.nytimes.com/1960/10/07/archives/prospect-park-rink-approved-wollman-fund-gives-300000.html|url-status=live}}</ref> To make the park more visually appealing, NYC Parks also began to clear the area of weeds and invasive species, though this had the unintended effect of hastening erosion.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Illson 1959" /><ref name="Martin 1998">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/09/14/nyregion/prospect-park-s-ravine-inching-closer-to-past.html|title=Prospect Park's Ravine Inching Closer to Past|last=Martin|first=Douglas|date=September 14, 1998|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216035237/https://www.nytimes.com/1998/09/14/nyregion/prospect-park-s-ravine-inching-closer-to-past.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

It was not unusual in the Moses years, and especially the decade after his departure, to quietly remove underutilized or redundant structures. To do so was regarded as economical and prudent management. Several structures had been destroyed by the time Moses left his position as NYC Parks commissioner in May 1960. These included the Dairy, destroyed 1935;<ref name="Lancaster" /> Concert Grove House, demolished 1949;<ref name="ConcertGroveHouse">{{cite web|year=2008|title=Concert Grove History|url=http://www.prospectpark.org/visit/history/historic_places/h_concert_grove|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090323073036/http://www.prospectpark.org/visit/history/historic_places/h_concert_grove|archive-date=March 23, 2009|access-date=March 21, 2009|publisher=Prospect Park Alliance}}</ref> Music Island, razed 1960;<ref name="Dunlap 2012" /><ref name="New York City Department of Parks & Recreation 2012" /> the Flower Garden;<ref name="am New York 2014" /> the Thatched Shelter, destroyed in the 1940s;<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Forgotten New York 2005" /> the Model Yacht Club, burned down in 1956;<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Forgotten New York 2005" /> and the Greenhouse Conservatories, taken apart in 1955.<ref name="Green" />

=== Late 20th century ===

==== 1960s and 1970s ====
The demolition of [[Pennsylvania Station (1910–1963)|Pennsylvania Station]] in Manhattan during 1963–1968 spawned a nascent [[historic preservation]] movement.<ref>{{cite web|title=Laying the Preservation Framework: 1960–1980|website=Cultural Landscapes (U.S. National Park Service)|date=April 24, 1962|url=https://www.nps.gov/subjects/culturallandscapes/cltimeline4.htm|access-date=September 6, 2018|archive-date=September 6, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180906202407/https://www.nps.gov/subjects/culturallandscapes/cltimeline4.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> In September 1964, the Parks Department was within forty-eight hours of demolishing the [[Boathouse on the Lullwater of the Lake in Prospect Park|Boathouse on the Lullwater]].<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Boathouse">{{cite web|url=http://www.prospectpark.org/visit/history/historic_places/h_boathouse|title=Audubon Center – History|year=2008|publisher=Prospect Park Alliance|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090321061145/http://www.prospectpark.org/visit/history/historic_places/h_boathouse|archive-date=March 21, 2009|url-status=dead|access-date=March 21, 2009}}</ref> At the time the structure was underutilized; the boat concession only operated on weekends and its peak traffic was fewer than ten people per hour.<ref name="NYTimes">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/09/19/archives/future-is-unsure-for-prospect-parks-old-boathouse-a-gaslight-relic.html|title=A Gaslight Relic Awaits Verdict; Prospect Park Boathouse May Face Demolition|last=Tolchin|first=Martin|date=September 14, 1964|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=August 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190821003141/https://www.nytimes.com/1964/09/19/archives/future-is-unsure-for-prospect-parks-old-boathouse-a-gaslight-relic.html|url-status=live}}</ref> However, the Boathouse shared many architectural design features with the famous station.  A preservation group, The Friends of Prospect Park, including in its membership, poet and longtime Brooklyn resident [[Marianne Moore]],<ref name="MMoore">{{cite book|last=Graff|first=M. M.|author2=George Kalmbacher|title=''Tree Trails of Prospect Park''|publisher=Greensward Foundation|year=1982|location=New York}}</ref> built public awareness over disappearing historical structures and threatened flora within the park. Public pressure induced Park Commissioner [[Newbold Morris]] to rescind the decision to demolish the Boathouse in December 1964.<ref name="NYTimesSave">{{cite news|last=Tolchin|first=Martin|title=Boathouse Saved At Prospect Park; Morris 'Succumbs to Public Opinion' on Landmark|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|date=December 11, 1964|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/09/19/archives/future-is-unsure-for-prospect-parks-old-boathouse-a-gaslight-relic.html|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=August 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190821003141/https://www.nytimes.com/1964/09/19/archives/future-is-unsure-for-prospect-parks-old-boathouse-a-gaslight-relic.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

Projects to restore Prospect Park were taken up by the late 1960s. In 1965, the city allocated $450,000 to renovate the Vale of Cashmere and the Rose Garden ahead of Brooklyn's 300th anniversary, and the park's 100th anniversary, the following year.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1965/08/08/archives/city-will-spruce-up-brooklyns-prospect-park-in-a-450000-project.html|title=City Will Spruce Up Brooklyn's Prospect Park in a $450,000 Project|date=August 8, 1965|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 16, 2019|archive-date=February 17, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190217032014/https://www.nytimes.com/1965/08/08/archives/city-will-spruce-up-brooklyns-prospect-park-in-a-450000-project.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Another $225,000 was allocated to renovate the boathouse, and $249,000 was allotted to overall renovations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1965/01/01/archives/restoration-due-in-prospect-park-planners-vote-924000-citizens.html|title=Restoration Due In Prospect Park; Planners Vote $924,000 -Citizens' Group Hailed|last=Tolchin|first=Martin|date=December 1, 1964|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 16, 2019|archive-date=February 17, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190217084926/https://www.nytimes.com/1965/01/01/archives/restoration-due-in-prospect-park-planners-vote-924000-citizens.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The city renovated part of the Long Meadow on the northwest side of the park, as well as the children's farm. However, some of the contracts were delayed, including renovations to the Boathouse and the tennis courts, as well as a reconstruction of the Music Pagoda, which had burned down in 1968.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28132742/|title=Rap City for Lagging on Repairs to Prospect Park|date=April 5, 1970|work=New York Daily News|access-date=February 7, 2019|page=109|via=Newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041208/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-rap-city-for-lagging-on-repai/28132742/|url-status=live}}</ref> By 1971, the city had spent $4 million to renovate Prospect Park, including renovating the Boathouse and dredging the lake. The Rose Garden and the Vale of Cashmere had also been re-landscaped.<ref name="Knight 1971">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1971/02/28/archives/prospect-parks-future-is-pondered-a-place-to-play-or-a-place-to.html|title=Prospect Park's Future Is Pondered: A Place to Play or a Place to Find Tranquillity?|last=Knight|first=Michael|date=February 28, 1971|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201065457/https://www.nytimes.com/1971/02/28/archives/prospect-parks-future-is-pondered-a-place-to-play-or-a-place-to.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Also part of the renovation was a restoration of the Prospect Park Carousel from 1971 to 1974,<ref name="Cadkin 1974">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/10/13/archives/park-carousel-reopening.html|title=Park Carousel Reopening|last=Cadkin|first=Janice C.|date=October 13, 1974|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215220048/https://www.nytimes.com/1974/10/13/archives/park-carousel-reopening.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and the exterior of the Boathouse was restored in 1979.<ref name="Gray 1996">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/06/30/realestate/streetscapes-prospect-park-boathouse-after-1971-restoration-fails-it-s-time-re.html|title=Streetscapes/Prospect Park Boathouse;After a 1971 Restoration Fails, It's Time to Re-Restore|last=Gray|first=Christopher|date=June 30, 1996|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209124502/https://www.nytimes.com/1996/06/30/realestate/streetscapes-prospect-park-boathouse-after-1971-restoration-fails-it-s-time-re.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

By the 1970s, Prospect Park was beset by crime; a 1974 report found that 44 percent of city residents would warn people to stay away from the park under any circumstances.<ref name="Dailey 2013" />  Much of Prospect Park suffered soil erosion and lack of maintenance caused the landscape to deteriorate. By 1979, park attendance dropped to two million, the lowest recorded level in the history of the park.<ref name="PPAHistory" />

==== 1980s and 1990s ====
The mayoral administration of [[Ed Koch]] formed plans in 1980 to turn over the administration of the troubled [[Prospect Park Zoo]] to the [[Wildlife Conservation Society]].<ref name="NYZooTakeOver">{{cite news|title=City's 3 Zoos to Be Taken Over By New York Zoological Society|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|date=April 23, 1980|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1980/04/23/archives/citys-3-zoos-to-be-taken-over-by-new-york-zoological-society-citys.html|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=April 22, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190422194221/https://www.nytimes.com/1980/04/23/archives/citys-3-zoos-to-be-taken-over-by-new-york-zoological-society-citys.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Over the next seven years, the city invested $17 million in cleaning up the park,<ref name="NYTimes-PPA-Creation-1987" /> including $10 million in federal funds from a [[Community Development Block Grant]].<ref name="Laskow 2014">{{Cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/states/new-york/city-hall/story/2016/05/what-donors-do-for-some-city-parks-047653|title=What donors do for (some) city parks|last=Laskow|first=Sarah|date=June 30, 2014|newspaper=Politico PRO|access-date=January 10, 2017|archive-date=February 15, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170215032200/http://www.politico.com/states/new-york/city-hall/story/2016/05/what-donors-do-for-some-city-parks-047653|url-status=live}}</ref> Annual visitor numbers had nearly tripled to 5 million between 1980 and 1987.<ref name="NYTimes-PPA-Creation-1987" /> During this period, Prospect Park also received two historic designations: it was made a [[New York City scenic landmark]] on November 25, 1975,<ref name="nycl" /> and was listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] on September 17, 1980.<ref name="nris" />

The Prospect Park Alliance, a non-profit organization, was created in April 1987 based on the model of the [[Central Park Conservancy]], which had helped restore Central Park in the 1980s. Shortly afterward, NYC Parks began entering into restoration projects with the organization.<ref name="NYTimes-PPA-Creation-1987">{{cite web|last=Anderson|first=Susan Heller|title=Nonprofit Group To Nourish Once-Shabby Prospect Park|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|date=April 6, 1987|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/04/06/nyregion/nonprofit-group-to-nourish-once-shabby-prospect-park.html|access-date=February 10, 2019|archive-date=February 10, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190210152600/https://www.nytimes.com/1987/04/06/nyregion/nonprofit-group-to-nourish-once-shabby-prospect-park.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The Alliance's first major project was the $550,000 restoration of the Carousel in 1987–1989. The carousel had not operated since 1983, and its original horse-shaped seats were removed during the restoration.<ref name="Martin 1989">{{cite web|last=Martin|first=Douglas|title=About New York; Restoring Some Magic To Brooklyn|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|date=October 7, 1989|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/10/07/nyregion/about-new-york-restoring-some-magic-to-brooklyn.html|access-date=February 10, 2019|archive-date=February 10, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190210152659/https://www.nytimes.com/1989/10/07/nyregion/about-new-york-restoring-some-magic-to-brooklyn.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Nine years later, in 1996, it started a $4.5 million restoration of the Ravine.<ref name="LastForest" /><ref name="Dailey 2013" /> The Boathouse was also restored again in the late 1990s due to deterioration of the exterior terracotta.<ref name="Gray 1996" /> The [[National Audubon Society]] signed a lease for the Boathouse in 2000,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/04/30/nyregion/neighborhood-report-prospect-park-bird-lovers-will-find-home-beaux-arts.html|title=Neighborhood Report: Prospect Park; Bird Lovers Will Find a Home in a Beaux-Arts Boathouse|last=Bahrampour|first=Tara|date=April 30, 2000|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215220026/https://www.nytimes.com/2000/04/30/nyregion/neighborhood-report-prospect-park-bird-lovers-will-find-home-beaux-arts.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and the building became the site of the nation's first urban Audubon society.<ref name="auduboncenter">{{cite web|url=http://ny.audubon.org/CentersEdu_ProspectPark.html|title=Audubon New York|year=2008|publisher=National Audubon Society|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090116062220/http://ny.audubon.org/CentersEdu_ProspectPark.html|archive-date=January 16, 2009|url-status=dead|access-date=November 29, 2008}}</ref> The restoration of the Harmony Playground and Bandshell was completed the same year.<ref name="Harmony Playground : NYC Parks 1939">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/highlights/11884|title=Prospect Park Highlights|date=June 26, 1939|website=Harmony Playground : NYC Parks|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216035435/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/highlights/11884|url-status=live}}</ref> However, other parts of Prospect Park remained neglected, such as the eastern side of the park, where the surrounding community was generally poorer than the western side.<ref>{{cite news|last=Brick|first=Michael|title=A Park Pretty for the Rich Yet Run-Down for the Poor; Prospect Park Overseers Direct Money To Make East Side More Like the West|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|date=May 27, 2004|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/05/27/nyregion/park-pretty-for-rich-yet-run-down-for-poor-prospect-park-overseers-direct-money.html|access-date=March 28, 2019|archive-date=March 28, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190328034043/https://www.nytimes.com/2004/05/27/nyregion/park-pretty-for-rich-yet-run-down-for-poor-prospect-park-overseers-direct-money.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Early 21st century ===

==== 2000s and 2010s ====
[[File:Prospect Park Brooklyn Feb 2019 57.jpg|thumb|A promenade facing the lake, built in the first decade of the 21st century]]

By 2000, the Wollman Rink was deteriorating, and there was a need to replace it.<ref name="Bahrampour 2000">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/12/03/nyregion/neighborhood-report-prospect-park-brooklyn-s-prized-wollman-rink-feeling-its-age.html|title=Neighborhood Report: Prospect Park; Brooklyn's Prized Wollman Rink Is Feeling Its Age|last=Bahrampour|first=Tara|date=December 3, 2000|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201014943/https://www.nytimes.com/2000/12/03/nyregion/neighborhood-report-prospect-park-brooklyn-s-prized-wollman-rink-feeling-its-age.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The Alliance soon formed plans to restore Music Island and the original shoreline, both obliterated by the construction of the original rink in 1960.<ref name="PPAAnnual2006">{{cite book|title=''Prospect Park Alliance Annual Report 2006''|publisher=Prospect Park Alliance|year=2006|page=9|location=New York|url=http://www.prospectpark.org/general/annual_reports/AR2006.pdf|format=PDF (Portable Document Format)|access-date=March 21, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080228210632/http://www.prospectpark.org/general/annual_reports/AR2006.pdf|archive-date=February 28, 2008}}
</ref><ref name="Curr">{{cite web|year=2008|title=Wollman Rink|access-date=March 21, 2009|publisher=Prospect Park Alliance|url=http://www.prospectpark.org/visit/history/historic_places/h_wollman_rink|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090220130535/http://www.prospectpark.org/visit/history/historic_places/h_wollman_rink|archive-date=February 20, 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref> Several Moses-era playgrounds and the Bandshell were retained because their venues were popular. Original rustic summer houses were restored or recreated on the shores of Prospect Park Lake, along the Lullwater and in the Ravine.<ref name="Lakeside" /> As part of the restoration plans, the
