==Geography==
{{Prospect Park (Brooklyn)}}
Prospect Park occupies {{convert|526|acre|ha|abbr=}} in central Brooklyn. It is bound by Prospect Park West and the neighborhood of [[Park Slope]] to the northwest; Prospect Park Southwest and the [[Windsor Terrace, Brooklyn|Windsor Terrace]] neighborhood to the southwest and west; Parkside Avenue, [[Ocean Avenue (Brooklyn)|Ocean Avenue]], [[Flatbush Avenue]], and the neighborhood of [[Flatbush]] to the south and southeast; and [[Grand Army Plaza]] and the neighborhood of [[Prospect Heights, Brooklyn|Prospect Heights]] to the north.<ref name="parkstat">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/prospect-park|title=Prospect Park|date=June 26, 1939|publisher=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=January 28, 2019|archive-date=November 19, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181119153001/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/prospect-park|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Design ===
Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux engineered Prospect Park to recreate in real space the pastoral, picturesque, and aesthetic ideals expressed in contemporary paintings.<ref name="nycl"/>{{rp|3}}<ref name="Tate 2015 p. 220" />{{Rp|219–220}} The overall design was inspired partially by [[Birkenhead Park]] in the United Kingdom.<ref name="Dailey 2013" /> Prospect Park had recent precedents in the pastoral style, notably [[Mount Auburn Cemetery]] near Boston and [[Green-Wood Cemetery]] a few blocks away.<ref name="Bluestone 1987" /> Olmsted and Vaux felt they had greater success in Brooklyn because of the lack of obstacles there, but they were also assisted in part by park commissioner James Stranahan's patronage and support of their plan.<ref name="Tate 2015 p. 220" />{{Rp|219–220}}

The two designers wanted visitors to be able to traverse Prospect Park with a myriad of perspectives so that the features could be enjoyed in any order.<ref name="Bluestone 1987" /> Olmsted was more involved with the general design of Prospect Park, while Vaux was more involved with specific details.<ref name="Dailey 2013" /> They created the large Long Meadow out of hilly upland pasture interspersed with peat bogs. They also moved and planted trees, hauled topsoil and created a vast unfolding turf with trees placed both separately and in groups. The designers wanted Lookout Hill to be a place of broad views out over Prospect Lake, the farmland beyond, and the bay and ocean in the distance.<ref name="Lancaster" /> To create an illusion of an expansive space, Olmsted and Vaux designed the paths in Prospect Park to be meandering.<ref name="Dailey 2013" />

=== Layout ===
In Olmsted and Vaux's final plan for the park, it was divided into three distinct zones: an open section, a wooded section, and a waterside section. The Parade Ground at the far southwestern corner was excluded from the system of zones.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Bluestone 1987" /><ref name="Gray 1994">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/07/17/realestate/streetscapes-prospect-park-the-other-olmsted-vaux-landscape-masterpiece.html|title=Streetscapes/Prospect Park; The Other Olmsted & Vaux Landscape Masterpiece|last=Gray|first=Christopher|date=July 17, 1994|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 28, 2019|archive-date=January 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129012110/https://www.nytimes.com/1994/07/17/realestate/streetscapes-prospect-park-the-other-olmsted-vaux-landscape-masterpiece.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The first zone consisted of the Long Meadow, a wide open space along the west side of the park.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018">{{Cite map|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/media/filer_public/fc/df/fcdf91e9-eb0b-4663-a163-541f79c51c88/prospect_park_map.pdf|title=Prospect Park Alliance Map|publisher=Prospect Park Alliance|date=2018|access-date=January 28, 2019|archive-date=August 10, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190810024340/https://www.prospectpark.org/media/filer_public/fc/df/fcdf91e9-eb0b-4663-a163-541f79c51c88/prospect_park_map.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> It contains two entrances through tunnels: Meadowport Arch and Endale Arch.<ref name="Gray 1994" /> The Third Street Playground, Harmony Playground, bandshell, and the picnic and tennis houses are also located here. West Drive traverses this section of Prospect Park.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" />

The second zone is the wooded area in the middle of the park and contains the headwaters of the park's watercourse. In this zone, on the northeast side of the park, there are several points of interest: the Ravine, the Vale of Cashmere, the Rose Garden, the Zucker Natural Exploration Area, and the [[Prospect Park Zoo]].<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The area contains the Nethermead Arch, an elaborate triple-span bridge.<ref name="Gray 1994" /> Quaker Hill and the Friends Cemetery are located near the southwest boundary of Prospect Park.<ref name="Biederman 1998">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/09/27/nyregion/neighborhood-report-prospect-park-park-slope-he-s-here-for-eternity-but-don-t.html|title=Neighborhood Report: Prospect Park/Park Slope; He's Here for Eternity, but Don't Ask Where|last=Biederman|first=Marcia|date=September 27, 1998|work=The New York Times|access-date=August 21, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=August 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190821161254/https://www.nytimes.com/1998/09/27/nyregion/neighborhood-report-prospect-park-park-slope-he-s-here-for-eternity-but-don-t.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Lookout Hill, as well as a large open space called the Nethermead, are located to the south and east of Quaker Hill, respectively.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The Ravine also contains the Midwood, an [[old-growth forest]] incorporated into Prospect Park during its construction.<ref name="LastForest" /><ref name="am New York 2014" /><ref name="Scherer 2017" />

The third zone is along the park's south side and consists of Prospect Lake, as well as a peninsula jutting eastward from the lake's northern shore.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> It is the outlet for the Lullwater, a meandering stream.<ref name="Gray 1994" /> The Lullwater contains the classical-style [[Boathouse on the Lullwater of the Lake in Prospect Park|Boathouse]], a city- and federally-designated landmark, on the Lullwater's eastern shore. To the south, along the lake's eastern shore, are the White Levy Esplanade, as well as the LeFrak Center at Lakeside, a multipurpose recreation center.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The LeFrak Center at Lakeside consists of a pair of one-story structures, which share a planted roof. The rink's ceiling contains abstract light-colored streaks on a blue background, which are intended to represent skaters' movements. Also part of the LeFrak Center is a building with a cafe, offices, and event space.<ref name="Bendov 2017 p. 124">{{cite book|last=Bendov|first=Pavel|title=New Architecture New York|publisher=Prestel Publishing|year=2017|isbn=978-3-7913-8368-2|publication-place=New York, NY|page=121|oclc=976405424}}</ref>

Parkside Avenue, a roughly west–east street, divides the southwestern part of Prospect Park from the rest of the park. This detached sliver of parkland is bounded by Parkside Avenue to the north, Coney Island Avenue to the west, Caton Avenue to the south, and Parade Place to the east. It contains the Parade Ground, which has fifteen numbered courts and fields for various sports.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" />

All of the waterways in Prospect Park are part of a single man-made watercourse. A winding naturalistic stream channel with several ponds feeds a {{Convert|60|acre|ha|abbr=|adj=on}} lake at the south end of the park.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> In designing the watercourse, Olmsted and Vaux also took advantage of the preexisting glacier-formed [[Kettle (geology)|kettle ponds]] and lowland outwash plains to create a [[drainage basin]] centered around the waterway. They crafted the watercourse to include a steep, forested Ravine with significant river edge flora and fauna habitats.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Brooklyn Paper 2011">{{cite web|url=https://www.brooklynpaper.com/stories/34/34/web_lloydletter_2011_8_26_bk.html|title=The Park is functioning as designed|last=Lloyd|first=Emily|date=August 26, 2011|website=Brooklyn Paper|access-date=February 13, 2019|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214002938/https://www.brooklynpaper.com/stories/34/34/web_lloydletter_2011_8_26_bk.html|url-status=live}}</ref> As a result, the watercourse is able to accommodate significant bird and fish populations.<ref name="Prospect Park 1939">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/highlights/11760|title=Prospect Park Highlights – the Wetlands of New York City : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=Prospect Park|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=October 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211014152018/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/highlights/11760|url-status=live}}</ref>

Much of the watercourse is lined with vegetation that is designed to absorb precipitation and additional water flow.<ref name="Brooklyn Paper 2011" /> Olmsted also included an expansive drainage system, which is still in use and extends under the Long Meadow, Ravine, and Nethermead.<ref name="Dailey 2013" /> About two-thirds of Prospect Park Lake's water typically evaporates. However, to prevent flooding after heavy precipitation, Prospect Park employees can control the outflow of water from the lake using a valve.<ref name="Brooklyn Paper 2011" /><ref name="Pollak 2009">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/15/nyregion/15fyi.html|title=Take That, E-Mail|last=Pollak|first=Michael|date=November 15, 2009|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 13, 2019|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214003038/https://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/15/nyregion/15fyi.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

By the mid-20th century, these artificial waterways and the steep slopes around them had lost their original design character.  In 1994, the Prospect Park Alliance launched a 25-year $43-million restoration project for the watercourse.<ref name="LastForest" />

==== Smaller waterways ====
The water in Prospect Park originates at the top of Fallkill Falls in the center of the park, just north of Quaker Hill and east of Long Meadow.<ref name="Kadinsky20162">{{cite Hidden Waters NYC|pages=226–229}}</ref><ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" />  The [[Prospect Park (Brooklyn)#Well House|Well House]] on the north side of the Lake originally provided the water for the watercourse, and was connected to an underground [[aquifer]].<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Brooklyn Paper 2011" /> The Well House became outdated when Prospect Park was connected to the [[New York City water supply system]] in the early 20th century.<ref name="Kadinsky20162" /><ref name="Warerkar 2017" /><ref name="Vries 2018">{{cite web|url=https://www.brownstoner.com/history/prospect-park-brooklyn-wellhouse-cistern-calvert-vaux-prospect-park-alliance/|title=Take a Seat on a Piece of Engineering History in Prospect Park|last=De Vries|first=Susan|date=June 20, 2018|website=Brownstoner|access-date=February 2, 2019|archive-date=February 2, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190202095549/https://www.brownstoner.com/history/prospect-park-brooklyn-wellhouse-cistern-calvert-vaux-prospect-park-alliance/|url-status=live}}</ref> By the 21st century, Fallkill Falls was fed by a pipe from the city's water system.<ref name="Brooklyn Paper 2011" /><ref name="Pollak 2009" />

[[File:Prospect Park New York May 2015 009.jpg|thumb|left|Binnen waterfall]]
The water from Fallkill Falls runs into Fallkill Pool, past the Fallkill Bridge, through the Upper Pool and Lower Pool, where migratory birds rest and marsh and other water plants can be found.<ref name="Kadinsky20162" /> The Upper Pool abuts a dog beach, while the Long Meadow is adjacent to the Lower Pool.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The water then passes under the Esdale Bridge, a footbridge over Ambergill Pond. The pond, and the Ambergill Falls just past it, was named by Olmsted and refers to the [[Gill (ravine)|Old Norse word for "creek"]].<ref name="Kadinsky20162" /> After passing through Ambergill Falls, the water flows under Rock Arch Bridge and past the Ravine, entering the Binnenwater, which is named after a Dutch word for "within".<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|64}}<ref name="Kadinsky20162" /> The waters then cascade beneath the Binnen Bridge to the Lullwater, a small pond that contains the Boathouse on its eastern bank. The water then flows under the Lullwater and Terrace bridges to the Peninsula, which is managed both as bird sanctuary and recreational field.<ref name="Kadinsky20162" /><ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" />

==== Lake ====
[[File:Prospect Park lake.jpeg|thumb|Prospect Park's lake]]
The mouth of Prospect Park's watercourse is the artificial, 60-acre Prospect Lake (also known as Prospect Park Lake).<ref name="Prospect Park 1939" /> Prospect Lake includes several islands and is home to over 20 species of fish. Every year, the lake hosts the R.H. Macy's Fishing Contest,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://nymag.com/family/kids/17391/|title=Go Fish|last=Avery|first=Susan|date=July 10, 2006|website=NYMag.com|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=August 5, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805114955/https://nymag.com/family/kids/17391/|url-status=live}}</ref> a tradition that dates to 1947.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cityroom.blogs.nytimes.com/2007/07/18/go-fish-trying-to-land-a-big-one-in-prospect-park/|title=Go Fish: Trying to Land a Big One in Prospect Park|last=Chan|first=Sewell|date=July 18, 2016|website=City Room|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=October 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191007160414/https://cityroom.blogs.nytimes.com/2007/07/18/go-fish-trying-to-land-a-big-one-in-prospect-park/|url-status=live}}</ref> Though NYC Parks generally allows licensed anglers to fish, it maintains a [[catch and release]] policy to prevent depletion of the fish population.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/07/08/sports/othersports/08outdoors.html|title=Catch This! Lake Full of Largemouth Only a Subway Ride Away|last=Skog|first=Jason|date=July 8, 2006|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209124206/https://www.nytimes.com/2006/07/08/sports/othersports/08outdoors.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In addition, visitors may explore the lake in [[kayak]]s and [[Pedalo|pedal boats]], available at the LeFrak Center at Lakeside,<ref name="PP-Pedalboats">{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/visit-the-park/things-to-do/boating/|title=Boating in Prospect Park|website=Prospect Park|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=March 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190315224757/https://www.prospectpark.org/visit-the-park/things-to-do/boating/|url-status=live}}</ref> or the ''Independence,'' a replica of the original [[Electric boat|electric launch]] which took day-trippers around the lake in the 20th century.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.timeout.com/newyork/things-to-do/audubon-center-at-the-boathouse|title=Audubon Center at the Boathouse – Things to do in Prospect Park, Brooklyn|date=March 7, 2011|website=Time Out New York|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209124252/https://www.timeout.com/newyork/things-to-do/audubon-center-at-the-boathouse|url-status=live}}</ref> On the shore of the lake, there are several "rustic shelters" that provide scenic views of the water.<ref name="Forgotten New York 2005">{{cite web|url=https://forgotten-ny.com/2005/05/secrets-of-prospect-park/|title=Secrets of Prospect Park|date=May 30, 2005|website=Forgotten New York|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209123946/https://forgotten-ny.com/2005/05/secrets-of-prospect-park/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Ice skating, popularized in Central Park, was a key reason for including Prospect Lake in the design of the park's watercourse.<ref name="Lancaster" /> In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, red balls raised on the fronts of [[Tram|trolley]] cars signified that the ice was at least four inches thick.<ref name="Iceskate">{{cite news|title=Ball Goes Up Again|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|page=17|date=January 9, 1900|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50380935/|access-date=February 20, 2018|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214002940/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50380935/|url-status=live}}</ref> Red flags were also placed at Grand Army Plaza to indicate the ice's sufficient thickness.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/news-events/news/archives-skating-through-history/|title=From the Archives: Skating through History|date=January 22, 2019|website=Prospect Park|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216153227/https://www.prospectpark.org/news-events/news/archives-skating-through-history/|url-status=live}}</ref> Later, green flags were used to indicate that the ice was thick enough, and red flags indicated that the ice was too thin. Since then, safety concerns have ended skating on the lake; as a result of [[climate change]], winters have become warmer in the 21st century compared to the 19th century, the ice on the lake has become too thin to accommodate skaters.<ref name="Bahrampour 2000" /> Ice skating moved to the Kate Wollman Rink in 1960, and again to the Lakeside Center in 2012.<ref name="Lakeside" />

===The Ravine===
[[File:Prospect Park Brooklyn Mar 2019 79.jpg|thumb|View of the watercourse inside the Ravine]]

A {{convert|146|acre|adj=on}} section of Prospect Park's interior is known as the Ravine.<ref name="NewsTimes 2009">{{cite news|title=New life for Prospect Park|work=The News-Times|location=Danbury, CT|date=November 24, 2009|url=https://www.newstimes.com/news/article/New-life-for-Prospect-Park-47222.php|access-date=November 20, 2023|archive-date=November 20, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231120222758/https://www.newstimes.com/news/article/New-life-for-Prospect-Park-47222.php|url-status=live|last=Miller|first=Robert}}</ref><ref name="TCLF">{{cite web|title=Prospect Park|website=[[The Cultural Landscape Foundation]]|url=https://www.tclf.org/landscapes/prospect-park|access-date=November 20, 2023|archive-date=November 20, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231120222758/https://www.tclf.org/landscapes/prospect-park|url-status=live}}</ref> The region contains the headwaters of the park's water system, as well as Brooklyn's only remaining old-growth forest, the Midwood.<ref name="LastForest" /><ref name="am New York 2014" /><ref name="Scherer 2017" /> Olmsted and Vaux saw the Ravine as the heart of Prospect Park and the centerpiece of mountainous tableaux similar to the [[Adirondack Mountains]],<ref>{{cite web|last=Jacobs|first=Harrison|date=November 22, 2013|url=http://www.businessinsider.com/photos-of-prospect-parks-top-sites-2013-11?op=1|title=29 Reasons Why Prospect Park Is The Best In New York|website=businessinsider.com|access-date=March 20, 2018|archive-date=March 21, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180321130525/http://www.businessinsider.com/photos-of-prospect-parks-top-sites-2013-11?op=1|url-status=live}}</ref> and designed it in a similar fashion to their [[The Ramble and Lake|Ramble in Central Park]].<ref name="Kadinsky20162" /> The perimeter of the area is a steep, narrow {{convert|100|ft|m|abbr=|adj=on}} gorge.  The watercourse goes through the Ravine en route to the Boathouse.<ref name="ravinehistory" />

The original design of the Ravine was more aesthetic than functional, and decades of deferred maintenance had degraded the Ravine and made it hard to drain. During the 1970s, the brush was trimmed in order to make it harder for muggers to hide, and by the 1990s, the stream had dried up.<ref name="Dailey 2013" /> In 1996, still recovering from decades of overuse that caused soil compaction and erosion, the Ravine and surrounding woodlands underwent a $4.5 million restoration.<ref name="LastForest" /><ref name="Martin 1998" /> The Ravine was opened for tours two years later.<ref name="Martin 1998" /><ref name="ravinehistory" /> By 2002, part of the Ravine had been restored and opened to the public.<ref name="ravinehistory">{{cite web|url=http://www.prospectpark.org/about-prospect-park/history/historic-places/ravine|title=Ravine District history|website=prospectpark.org|access-date=March 20, 2018|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140713042639/http://www.prospectpark.org/about-prospect-park/history/historic-places/ravine|archive-date=July 13, 2014}}</ref>

Directly south of the Ravine is a [[meadow#Urban meadow|meadow]] called the Nethermead, which occupies much of the space along the western bank of the watercourse between Center and Wellhouse Drive.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018"/> To the southwest of the Nethermead is Lookout Hill, which occupies the remaining area between Center and Wellhouse Drives.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018"/>

{{wide image|ProspectPark Brooklyn Nethermead.jpg|750px|Southward view from the Nethermead Arches toward the Nethermead}}

=== Long Meadow ===
[[File:A walk in the park (49086734093).jpg|thumb|200px|A man and his dog enter Long Meadow from the west]]
The Long Meadow stretches down the western side of Prospect Park.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The meadow contains two playgrounds, the Tennis House, the Picnic House, a bandshell, a dog beach, and NYC Parks maintenance facilities.<ref name="Lancaster" /> In a contrast with the Ravine and the watercourse, the Long Meadow is mostly flat open space. As designed, it provided a visual buffer between the neighborhoods to the west and the interior of the park. During construction, Olmsted laid out hundreds of trees in meticulous patterns around the meadow.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Jacobs 2017">{{cite web|url=https://ny.curbed.com/2017/7/12/15953944/prospect-park-150-frederick-law-olmsted|title=The manhole in the meadow|last=Jacobs|first=Karrie|date=July 12, 2017|website=Curbed NY|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216035500/https://ny.curbed.com/2017/7/12/15953944/prospect-park-150-frederick-law-olmsted|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Originally, the Long Meadow hosted sports such as archery,<ref name="Dailey 2013" /> croquet,<ref name="The New York Times 2014" /> bowling, football, baseball, and tennis.<ref name="Lancaster" /> To preserve the meadow's pastoral quality, sheep grazed on the meadow until the 1930s.<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|16}}<ref name="Jacobs 2017" /> Today, much of the Long Meadow is used for a variety of purposes.<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|16}}<ref name="NYTimes-EnjoyPP-2018"/> The southern part of the Long Meadow contains seven baseball fields.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /><ref name="NYTimes-EnjoyPP-2018">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/19/travel/prospect-park-brooklyn-new-york.html|title=How to Enjoy Brooklyn's Prospect Park|last=Dorman|first=John L.|date=June 19, 2018|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216035602/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/19/travel/prospect-park-brooklyn-new-york.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Fauna and flora ==
[[File:Camperdown Elm (30405p).jpg|left|thumb|Prospect Park's Camperdown Elm]]
{{As of|2018||df=|since=}}, Prospect Park had 30,000 trees, comprising around 200 unique species.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bkreader.com/2018/10/02/survey-reveals-eco-benefits-and-value-of-prospect-park-trees/|title=Survey Reveals Eco Benefits and Value of Prospect Park Trees|last=Leonhardt|first=Andrea|date=October 2, 2018|website=BK Reader|access-date=February 5, 2019|archive-date=December 9, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211209092704/https://www.bkreader.com/2018/10/02/survey-reveals-eco-benefits-and-value-of-prospect-park-trees/|url-status=dead}}</ref> With few exceptions, the trees in Prospect Park were mostly planted manually. In its earliest years, Prospect Park had maintained a nursery of trees and plants, from which over a hundred thousand specimens were eventually taken.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Prospect Park">{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/learn-more/archives/park-tree-history/|title=The Tall History of Prospect Park's Trees|website=Prospect Park|access-date=February 5, 2019|archive-date=October 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211014191550/https://www.prospectpark.org/learn-more/archives/park-tree-history/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Now, Prospect Park Alliance regularly maintains the park's flora, removing [[invasive species]] and adding native plants.<ref name="Prospect Park" /> Prospect Park contains four "great trees" that are specially recognized by NYC Parks. These include a [[Ulmus glabra 'Camperdownii'|Camperdown Elm]] south of the Boathouse, among the first planted in the United States; an [[Carpinus caroliniana|American Hornbeam]] and a [[Styphnolobium japonicum|Japanese Pagodatree]] located near the Camperdown Elm; and an [[Ulmus minor 'Atinia'|English Elm]] along West Drive.<ref name="Prospect Park" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/news-events/news/results-are-in-prospect-park-tree-survey/|title=The Results Are In! Prospect Park Tree Survey|date=September 14, 2018|website=Prospect Park|access-date=February 5, 2019|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207015738/https://www.prospectpark.org/news-events/news/results-are-in-prospect-park-tree-survey/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/facilities/great-trees|title=Prospect Park Great Trees : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=February 5, 2019|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207015754/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/facilities/great-trees|url-status=live}}</ref> In late 2011, an [[oak]] tree was planted in the park as a memorial to Brooklyn native [[Peter Steele]], a member of the band [[Type O Negative]] who had died in 2010.<ref>{{cite web|last=Yakowicz|first=Will|title=Memorial for Peter Steele, Type O Negative Front Man, in Prospect Park|website=Park Slope, NY Patch|date=March 8, 2013|url=https://patch.com/new-york/parkslope/memorial-for-peter-steele-type-o-negative-front-man-i2f4762c8d9|access-date=April 14, 2023|archive-date=April 14, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230414232128/https://patch.com/new-york/parkslope/memorial-for-peter-steele-type-o-negative-front-man-i2f4762c8d9|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:PeterSteeleTree.jpg|thumb|An [[oak]] tree was planted in memory of [[Type O Negative]]'s [[Peter Steele]] in 2011 in Prospect Park. Fans of the band have hung tributes.]]

Prospect Park also accommodates a significant bird population. Each year, hundreds of migratory bird species stop at the park, and during winters, [[Birding in New York City|urban birdwatchers]] have reported seeing 60 unique species at the park on a good day, and 100 unique species over a typical season.<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|94}} Over the years, a total of 298 species have been recorded at Prospect Park, including 11 not seen at other city parks.<ref name="Buckley 2018">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PMpWDwAAQBAJ|title=Urban Ornithology: 150 Years of Birds in New York City|last1=Buckley|first1=P.A.|last2=Sedwitz|first2=W.|last3=Norse|first3=W.J.|last4=Kieran|first4=J.|publisher=Cornell University Press|year=2018|isbn=978-1-5017-1962-2|access-date=February 5, 2019|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041315/https://books.google.com/books?id=PMpWDwAAQBAJ|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|35}}  Though there are no official lists of birds that have been seen at the park, the Brooklyn Bird Club has kept records of the avian species seen there between 1967 and 1990.<ref name="Buckley 2018" />{{Rp|34–35}} Popular spots for birds included Lookout and Quaker Hills, the Ravine, the Vale of Cashmere, and Lily Pond.<ref name="Lancaster" />

[[File:Hawk with dead rodent in Prospect Park 01.jpg|thumb|A [[Red-tailed hawk]] with its [[rodent]] prey in Prospect Park]]

There are other fauna species in Prospect Park as well. In particular, the watercourse includes waterfowl, turtles, bullfrogs, fish, and crustacean species. In addition, squirrels are commonly seen in the park's trees.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|94}}<ref name="Prospect Park 1939" /> Sightings of butterflies are also common, and since the 1990s and 2000s, increasing numbers of bats have been seen in Prospect Park.<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|94}}

== Landmarks and structures ==
=== Plazas and entrances ===

Prospect Park is shaped roughly like a concave hexagon. There are three circles or plazas on the exterior corners of Prospect Park; all of these circles and plazas contain "major" park entrances.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2017" />{{Rp|7 (PDF p. 8)}}

====Major entrances====
[[Grand Army Plaza]] is an oval plaza at the northern corner, at the junction of Prospect Park West, [[Flatbush Avenue]], [[Eastern Parkway]], and several side streets. Olmsted and Vaux had intended for the plaza to be the park's main entrance, and it was constructed along with the park during the late 1860s.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50397475/|title=Prospect Park|date=June 20, 1867|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=February 5, 2019|page=2|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com|archive-date=June 12, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110612124953/http://eagle.brooklynpubliclibrary.org/Repository/getFiles.asp?Style=OliveXLib%3ALowLevelEntityToSaveGifMSIE_BEAGLE&Type=text%2Fhtml&Locale=english-skin-custom&Path=BEG%2F1867%2F06%2F20&ChunkNum=-1&ID=Ar00219|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="New York City Department of Parks & Recreation 1939 2">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B040/history|title=Grand Army Plaza Highlights : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=February 5, 2019|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207015324/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B040/history|url-status=live}}</ref> Grand Army Plaza's largest feature is the [[Soldiers' and Sailors' Arch]], a large [[triumphal arch]] in the center of the oval, which was dedicated in 1892. The plaza also includes four [[Doric order|Doric columns]], built 1894–1896; the ''[[Bailey Fountain]]'', constructed 1929–1932 on the site of two former fountains; and several statues of famous figures.<ref name="New York City Department of Parks & Recreation 1939 2" />

[[Bartel-Pritchard Square]], which is actually a circle, is at the far western corner of Prospect Park, at the junction of Prospect Park West and Southwest, where they turn into Ninth Avenue and 15th Street respectively. Dedicated with its present name in 1923, it is named after Brooklyn residents Emil Bartel and William Pritchard, who died in combat during [[World War I]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160304/windsor-terrace/how-bartel-pritchard-square-got-its-name-despite-being-circle-shaped|title=How Bartel-Pritchard 'Square' Got Its Name Despite Being Circle-Shaped|last=Levy|first=Nicole|date=March 4, 2016|website=DNAinfo New York|access-date=October 11, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011224216/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160304/windsor-terrace/how-bartel-pritchard-square-got-its-name-despite-being-circle-shaped|archive-date=October 11, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> The park entrance from the square was designed by Stanford White in 1896.<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|48}}

{{Anchor|Machate Circle}}Machate Circle is at the southwestern corner, at the junction of Prospect Park West, Ocean Parkway, and Parkside Avenue. Originally named Park Circle, it was renamed in 1989 in honor of a police officer killed in the line of duty. The park entrance from Machate Circle was also designed by Stanford White.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/machate-circle/history|title=Machate Circle Highlights : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=February 5, 2019|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207015711/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/machate-circle/history|url-status=live}}</ref>

Additional "major" entrances exist at the Parade Ground, on the park's south side; Parkside and Ocean Avenues, at the park's southeast corner; and [[Willink Plaza|Willink Hill]], at Flatbush and Ocean Avenues on the eastern border.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2017">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/lpc/downloads/pdf/presentation-materials/20171114/propsect-park-reduced.pdf|title=New Entrances for Prospect Park on Flatbush Avenue Located between Grand Army Plaza and the Prospect Park Zoo on Flatbush Avenue|last=Prospect Park Alliance|date=November 14, 2017|website=[[Government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=February 12, 2019|archive-date=February 13, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190213064113/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/lpc/downloads/pdf/presentation-materials/20171114/propsect-park-reduced.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|7 (PDF p. 8)}}<ref name="Prospect Park 2">{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/visit-the-park/park-map/park-entrances/|title=Park Entrances|website=Prospect Park|access-date=February 5, 2019|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207015957/https://www.prospectpark.org/visit-the-park/park-map/park-entrances/|url-status=live}}</ref> The Ocean/Parkside and Willink entrances were designed in the neoclassical style by McKim, Mead and White, and were built in the 1890s and 1900s. The Willink entrance is flanked by a pair of granite turrets, while the Ocean/Parkside entrance is located between the two portions of a curved granite colonnade.<ref name="Lancaster" /> Opposite the Willink entrance, there are the Flatbush Trees, three concrete cylinders with green sheet metal canopies, installed in 1979 and redecorated in 2015.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.brownstoner.com/neighborhood/prospect-lefferts-gardens/spring-has-finally-come-to-the-flatbush-trees/|title=Spring Has Finally Come to the Flatbush Trees|last=Scherer|first=Jeff|date=June 29, 2015|website=Brownstoner|language=en-US|access-date=July 21, 2019|archive-date=July 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190721164349/https://www.brownstoner.com/neighborhood/prospect-lefferts-gardens/spring-has-finally-come-to-the-flatbush-trees/|url-status=live}}</ref>

====Other entrances====
There are numerous other entrances spaced out along the park's border. These include five entrances on Prospect Park West, four on Prospect Park Southwest, and three on Ocean Avenue on the park's eastern border. In total, there are eighteen park entrances.<ref name="Prospect Park 2" /> Of these, the Third, Ninth, and 16th Street and Lincoln Road entrances are considered "major entrances", and are flanked by memorials or other decorations.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2017" />{{Rp|7 (PDF p. 8)}}  No entrances to Prospect Park have been built since the 1940s,<ref name="BKLYNER 2018" /> but two entrances were proposed for the Flatbush Avenue side in 2016 and are expected to be completed in mid-2020.<ref name="BKLYNER 2018" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/planning-and-building/capital-project-tracker/project/8647|title=Prospect Park New Flatbush Avenue Entrances Construction and Willink Entrance Reconstruction : NYC Parks|website=www.nycgovparks.org|access-date=July 21, 2019|archive-date=August 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190804051550/https://www.nycgovparks.org/planning-and-building/capital-project-tracker/project/8647|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== Bridges ===
==== Arches ====

Prospect Park originally included several arched bridges to provide grade-separated crossings for pedestrian and vehicular traffic; usually, the vehicular drive was located on top of the arch, and the pedestrian path was below.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Gray 2011">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/26/realestate/the-fate-of-prospect-parks-five-arches.html|title=The Fate of Prospect Park's Five Arches|last=Gray|first=Christopher|date=June 23, 2011|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 29, 2019|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130053144/https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/26/realestate/the-fate-of-prospect-parks-five-arches.html|url-status=live}}</ref> This contrasted with other parks at the time, which did not contain such separations. The arches were designed to be as small and natural-looking as possible so they did not interfere with the scenery.<ref name="nycl">{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0903.pdf|title=Prospect Park|date=November 25, 1975|publisher=Landmarks Preservation Commission|access-date=December 28, 2018|archive-date=December 23, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161223165332/http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0903.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|6}}<ref name="nyc.gov 1871" />{{Rp|39–40}} For the most part, the spaces under the arches were originally outfitted with benches, while the arches themselves blended with the foliage.<ref name="nyc.gov 1871" />{{Rp|40}} Five arched bridges were ultimately built, all during the late 1860s and early 1870s.<ref name="Lancaster" />

Endale Arch, also known as Enterdale Arch, is located under East Drive, slightly south of the Grand Army Plaza entrance on the north side of the park, and adjacent to the northeast side of Long Meadow.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /><ref name="Forgotten New York 2001">{{cite web|url=https://forgotten-ny.com/2001/08/the-bridges-of-prospect-park/|title=THE BRIDGES OF PROSPECT PARK|date=August 16, 2001|website=Forgotten New York|access-date=January 29, 2019|archive-date=January 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129235936/https://forgotten-ny.com/2001/08/the-bridges-of-prospect-park/|url-status=live}}</ref> It was one of the first two arches to be completed, in 1868. Its exterior contained interspersed yellow Ohio [[sandstone]] and red New Jersey [[brownstone]].<ref name="nycl" />{{Rp|6}}<ref name="Lancaster" /> The interior was composed of brick set between alternately black and yellow wooden stripes, designed as such to prevent condensation from dripping downward.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="nyc.gov 1871" />{{Rp|39–40}} Endale Arch contained seats underneath it, but these were later removed.<ref name="Gray 2011" /><ref name="Saraniero 2020"/> In 2014, the Prospect Park Alliance began a five-year restoration of the arch,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/news-events/news/endale-arch-restoration/|title=Endale Arch Restoration|date=November 20, 2014|website=Prospect Park|access-date=January 29, 2019|archive-date=January 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130053145/https://www.prospectpark.org/news-events/news/endale-arch-restoration/|url-status=live}}</ref> which was completed in 2020.<ref name="Saraniero 2020">{{Cite web|last=Saraniero|first=Nicole|date=November 16, 2020|title=Prospect Park's Endale Arch Magnificently Restored|url=https://untappedcities.com/2020/11/16/prospect-parks-endale-arch-magnificently-restored/|access-date=November 21, 2020|website=Untapped New York|language=en-US|archive-date=November 17, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201117020225/https://untappedcities.com/2020/11/16/prospect-parks-endale-arch-magnificently-restored/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Carlson|first=Jen|date=November 17, 2020|title=Inside The Beautifully Restored Endale Arch In Prospect Park|url=http://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment/endale-arch|access-date=November 21, 2020|website=Gothamist|language=en|archive-date=November 17, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201117205959/https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment/endale-arch|url-status=live}}</ref>

East Wood Arch (or Eastwood Arch) is also located under East Drive, connecting the Nethermead Arch to the Willink Hill entrance on the eastern side of Prospect Park.<ref name="nycl" />{{Rp|6}} It was the second of the two arches to be completed in 1868. East Wood Arch had a similar design to the Endale Arch, but had a simpler semicircular shape.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Forgotten New York 2001" />

Meadowport Arch is located on the northwest side of Long Meadow and passes under West Drive.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /><ref name="Forgotten New York 2001" /> It was completed in 1870.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Forgotten New York 2001" /> There were two portals at its eastern end, perpendicular to each other, creating a cross-vault. The arch had Ohio sandstone and wooden lining inside, and the portals contained circular [[cornice]]s, outward-facing [[Pier (architecture)|piers]], and octagonal domed [[finial]]s.<ref name="nycl" />{{Rp|6}}<ref name="Lancaster" /> Meadowport Arch was restored in the 1980s, but has since fallen into disrepair.<ref name="Gray 2011" />

Nethermead Arch, also completed {{Circa|}} 1870,<ref name="Lancaster" /> carries Center Drive through the center of the park.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /><ref name="Forgotten New York 2001" />  The bridge contains three arches: one each above the Ambergill, the park path, and the bridle path.<ref name="Forgotten New York 2001" /> The span is made of Ohio sandstone and contains a trim of granite.<ref name="nycl" />{{Rp|6}}<ref name="Lancaster" /> Unlike some of the other arches, Nethermead did not have any interior wood, but instead, had patterned red brick.<ref name="Gray 2011" /> ''The New York Times'' described its triple span as "one of the most astonishing structures in any city park".<ref name="Gray 1994" />

Cleft Ridge Span is located under Wellhouse Drive, at Breeze Hill, on the eastern side of Prospect Park.<ref name="nycl" />{{Rp|6}}<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> It was the final arch span to be opened, in 1872. The span was distinctive in its use of red, ochre, and pale gray concrete blocks called "Béton Coignet".<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Gray 2011" /><ref name="Chamberlin 1983">{{Cite journal|last=Chamberlin|first=William P.|date=1983|title=The Cleft-ridge Span: America's First Concrete Arch|journal=[[IA, The Journal of the Society for Industrial Archeology]]|volume=9|issue=1|pages=29–44|jstor=40968042}}</ref> Cleft Ridge might have been the first concrete arch span in the United States.<ref name="Chamberlin 1983" /> Both the interior and exterior designs were elaborate, though these have since eroded.<ref name="Lancaster" />

==== Other spans ====

Lullwater Bridge and Terrace Bridge are the only bridges across the watercourse that were built to handle automobile traffic.<ref name="Kadinsky20162" /> Lullwater Bridge is located just downstream of the [[Boathouse on the Lullwater of the Lake in Prospect Park|Boathouse]], on Prospect Park's eastern side.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The current metal span, built in 1905, replaces an oak bridge on the site that was originally constructed in 1868.<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|68–69}}<ref name="Forgotten New York 2001" /> Further downstream, Terrace Bridge carries Well House Drive over the watercourse just before it empties into the lake.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> Built in 1890, Terrace Bridge also replaced an earlier wooden span, and it contains cast-iron tracery and brick vaults underneath, which have since deteriorated.<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|70–71}}<ref name="Forgotten New York 2001" /> It was so named because it was supposed to overlook the unbuilt Refectory, which had been canceled following the 1873 financial crisis.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Kadinsky20162" />

From northwest to southeast, the Fallkill, Esdale, Nethermead Arch, Rock Arch, Music Grove, and Binnen Bridges also cross the watercourse upstream of the Lullwater Bridge. Fallkill, Esdale, and Rock Arch Bridges are located northwest of Nethermead Arch, while Music Grove and Binnen Bridges are located southeast of the arch.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /><ref name="Forgotten New York 2001" /> At the source of the watercourse, Fallkill and Esdale Bridges are both intended to look like wooden bridges, though are made of steel and concrete frames.<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|55}}<ref name="Forgotten New York 2001" /> Rock Arch Bridge, a boulder-lined span, crosses over Ambergill Falls; the waterfall had once been buried by the bridge's stonework, but was restored in the late 20th century when the bridge was rehabilitated.<ref name="PPGuide" />{{Rp|56}}<ref name="Forgotten New York 2001" /> To the south, Binnen Bridge and Music Grove Bridge were both designed as wood bridges.<ref name="Kadinsky20162" /> Binnen Bridge is located just north of the Lullwater, while Music Grove Bridge further upstream is located next to the Music Pagoda.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" />

=== Drives and paths ===
When it was built, Prospect Park did not have any transverse roadways. Instead, it was circled by a series of four scenic drives, named West, Center, Wellhouse, and East Drive.<ref name="nycl" />{{Rp|6}} The drives are paralleled by a more extensive system of pedestrian and bridle paths.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> Several paths in the park, as well as East Drive, follow ancient Native American trails.<ref name="am New York 2014" /><ref>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/stream/indianpathsingre01bolt/indianpathsingre01bolt_djvu.txt|title=Indian paths in the great metropolis|last=Bolton|first=Reginald Pelham|date=1922|access-date=February 7, 2019|via=Internet Archive}}</ref>

The drives were originally {{Convert|40|ft|m|abbr=}} wide and paved with gravel. The main loop, composed of West and East Drives, meanders around the park just inside its boundaries.<ref name="Lancaster" /> The loops were paved with asphalt and opened to automobiles in 1918.<ref name="Baker 2018">{{cite web|url=https://www.villagevoice.com/2018/01/02/prospect-park-is-car-free-at-last/|title=Prospect Park Is Car-Free At Last|last=Baker|first=R.C.|date=January 2, 2018|website=Village Voice|access-date=February 5, 2019|archive-date=September 12, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180912164140/https://www.villagevoice.com/2018/01/02/prospect-park-is-car-free-at-last/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Over the following decades, the hours at which vehicles could use the park were slowly restricted.<ref name="Voice cars">{{citation|author=Aaron Gordon|title=Prospect Park Is Car-Free at Last|date=January 2, 2018|url=https://www.villagevoice.com/2018/01/02/prospect-park-is-car-free-at-last/|publisher=[[The Village Voice]]|access-date=June 21, 2018|archive-date=June 22, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180622005046/https://www.villagevoice.com/2018/01/02/prospect-park-is-car-free-at-last/|url-status=dead}}</ref>  Supporters of a car ban argued that the park should be a haven from the type of city stress that automobiles represent, and that having them use the park sacrifices the safety of those using the park for [[recreation]],<ref name="Voice cars" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://transalt.org/campaigns/brooklyn/prospark.html|title=Transportation Alternatives Car-Free Prospect Park Campaign|website=transalt.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041207013458/http://www.transalt.org/campaigns/brooklyn/prospark.html|archive-date=December 7, 2004|url-status=dead|access-date=March 20, 2018}}</ref> while opponents worried that banning traffic in the park would increase traffic outside.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.brooklynpaper.com/stories/31/39/31_39_bm_let_em_drive.html |title=Locals: Keep Cars in Prospect Park |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081203145552/http://www.brooklynpaper.com/stories/31/39/31_39_bm_let_em_drive.html |archive-date=December 3, 2008 |work=Brooklyn Paper |date=October 2, 2008 |last=Meussig |first=Ben}}</ref>  The park's West Drive was closed to traffic in 2015.  Following a trial run in which the park was car-free during summer 2017, the city determined that there were no major effects on nearby routes, and cars were barred completely from the park beginning in January 2018.<ref name="Baker 2018" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://newyork.cbslocal.com/2018/01/02/prospect-park-car-ban-2/|title=Prospect Park Goes Permanently Car-Free|date=January 2, 2018|website=CBS New York|access-date=April 15, 2018|archive-date=April 16, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180416073751/http://newyork.cbslocal.com/2018/01/02/prospect-park-car-ban-2/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/local/Prospect-Park-Car-Free-Permanently-January-2018-452491093.html|title=Prospect Park Is Permanently Going Car-Free: Mayor|date=October 23, 2017|website=NBC 4 New York|access-date=June 21, 2018|archive-date=June 22, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180622005042/https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/local/Prospect-Park-Car-Free-Permanently-January-2018-452491093.html|url-status=live}}</ref> All of the drives are designated as [[protected bike lane]]s.<ref name="NYC Bike Map">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/html/dot/downloads/pdf/bikemap-2019.pdf|title=NYC DOT – Bicycle Maps|date=2019|website=[[Government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Transportation]]|access-date=May 14, 2019|archive-date=May 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190514162629/https://www1.nyc.gov/html/dot/downloads/pdf/bikemap-2019.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

There are also four hiking trails inside Prospect Park: the Lullwater, Midwood, Peninsula, and Waterfall trails. They range in length from {{Convert|0.5|to|1.0|mi|km|abbr=}}, and NYC Parks classifies all of the trails as "easy". The trails are named after the section of the park where they are located.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/facilities/hikingtrails|title=Prospect Park Hiking Trails : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=February 13, 2019|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214002754/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/facilities/hikingtrails|url-status=live}}</ref>
