Prospect Park contains dozens of monuments and statues to notable figures, including:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/|title=Prospect Park Monuments|date=June 26, 1939|website=NYC Parks|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214233415/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/|url-status=live}}</ref>
* A bronze statue of [[Abraham Lincoln]], sculpted by [[Henry Kirke Brown]] in 1869. Originally situated in Grand Army Plaza, it was relocated to the [[Concert Grove]] in Prospect Park in 1896, and restored in the late 1980s.<ref name="NYCParksLincoln">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/911|title=Abraham Lincoln|date=June 26, 1939|website=Abraham Lincoln : NYC Parks|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209124009/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/911|url-status=live}}</ref> With the Concert Grove's restoration in the 2010s, it was proposed to move the statue back to its original position,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052970203833104577070110343065918|title=In Brooklyn, G Marks the Spot for a Bust of Abe Lincoln|last=Newman|first=Barry|date=December 10, 2011|website=WSJ|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215050431/https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052970203833104577070110343065918|url-status=live}}</ref> but {{As of|2016||df=|lc=|since=}}, it was still located in the Concert Grove.<ref>{{cite web|title=Emancipation desecration! Prospect Park's historic Lincoln statue vandalized|website=Brooklyn Paper|last=Mixson|first=Colin|date=November 25, 2016|url=https://www.brooklynpaper.com/stories/39/48/dtg-prospect-park-lincoln-statue-vandalized-2016-11-25-bk.html|access-date=August 21, 2019|archive-date=August 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820194913/https://www.brooklynpaper.com/stories/39/48/dtg-prospect-park-lincoln-statue-vandalized-2016-11-25-bk.html|url-status=live}}</ref>
* A bronze-on-marble statue of [[James S.T. Stranahan]], sculpted by [[Frederick William MacMonnies|Frederick MacMonnies]] and located near the Grand Army Plaza entrance.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/1509|title=James S.T. Stranahan : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=Prospect Park Monuments|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=May 6, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506215056/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/1509|url-status=live}}</ref> It was dedicated in 1891 and honors Stranahan, one of the key figures in the park's development.<ref name="BrooklynEagleStranahan" />
* The [[Lafayette Memorial]], a bas-relief on granite at the Ninth Street entrance on the park's west side. The monument, which honors [[Marquis de Lafayette|Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette]], was sculpted by [[Daniel Chester French]] and was completed in 1917.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/883|title=Lafayette Memorial : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=Prospect Park Monuments|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=December 3, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201203051319/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/883|url-status=live}}</ref>
* The [[Maryland 400#Maryland 400 Monument|Maryland Monument]], a Corinthian column near Terrace Bridge. It was created by [[Stanford White]] and dedicated in 1895.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1895/02/04/archives/a-memorial-to-brave-marylanders.html|title=A Memorial to Brave Marylanders.|date=February 4, 1895|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190215050405/https://www.nytimes.com/1895/02/04/archives/a-memorial-to-brave-marylanders.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The column commemorates the [[Maryland 400]], members of the [[1st Maryland Regiment]] who charged British forces on Lookout Hill in the Battle of Long Island during the American Revolution, despite being outnumbered.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/highlights/19641|title=Maryland Monument : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=Prospect Park Highlights|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214233417/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/highlights/19641|url-status=live}}</ref>
* The Prospect Park War Memorial, along the eastern shore of the lake. Sculpted by [[Henry Augustus Lukeman]], it was dedicated in 1921. The memorial consists of two bronze figures in front of a curved wall with memorial plaques, containing the names of 2,800 people who died during [[World War I]].<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Prospect Park Monuments 1939">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/1229|title=Prospect Park War Memorial : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=Prospect Park Monuments|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214233431/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/1229|url-status=live}}</ref>
* Monuments to classical composers, including [[Ludwig van Beethoven|Beethoven]], [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart|Mozart]], and [[Carl Maria von Weber|von Weber]], in Concert Grove.<ref name="Scherer 2017" /><ref name="NYCParksVonWeber">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/1639|title=Von Weber Memorial : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=Prospect Park Monuments|access-date=February 14, 2019|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214233419/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/monuments/1639|url-status=live}}</ref> The surrounding area also contains tributes to poet [[Thomas Moore]], writer [[Washington Irving]], and classical composer [[Edvard Grieg]].<ref name="NYCParksVonWeber"/>
* A proposed monument of [[Shirley Chisholm]] at the Parkside and Ocean Avenues entrance. The design, by artists [[Amanda Williams (artist)|Amanda Williams]] and [[Olalekan Jeyifous]],<ref>{{Cite news|last=Steinhauer|first=Jillian|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/23/arts/design/shirley-chisholm-monument-prospect-park.html|title=The Shirley Chisholm Monument in Brooklyn Finds Its Designers|date=April 23, 2019|work=The New York Times|access-date=February 25, 2020|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=March 14, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200314084150/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/23/arts/design/shirley-chisholm-monument-prospect-park.html|url-status=live}}</ref> was approved by the city government in 2023.<ref>{{cite web | last=Small | first=Zachary | title=City Approves Design for Shirley Chisholm Monument in Prospect Park | website=The New York Times | issn=0362-4331 | date=July 17, 2023 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/07/17/arts/design/chisholm-monument-sculpture-approved.html | access-date=August 10, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Walton | first=Chris | title=Design for the Shirley Chisholm Monument gets approval | website=The Architect's Newspaper | date=July 25, 2023 | url=https://www.archpaper.com/2023/07/olalekan-jeyifous-amanda-williams-shirley-chisholm-monument-gets-approval/ | access-date=August 10, 2025}}</ref>

=== Notable structures ===
==== West side and Long Meadow ====
[[File:Litchfield Villa jeh.JPG|alt=Litchfield Villa, on the west side of the park|thumb|[[Litchfield Villa]], on the west side of the park]]
The [[Prospect Park Picnic House|Picnic House]] is located in Long Meadow on Prospect Park's west side.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> Built in 1927, it replaced an earlier rustic structure that had burned down the previous year.<ref name="PicnicHouse">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1926/04/26/archives/picnic-house-razed-by-fire-in-brooklyn-thousands-of-sunday.html|title=Picnic House Razed by Fire in Brooklyn|date=April 26, 1926|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=August 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190821003143/https://www.nytimes.com/1926/04/26/archives/picnic-house-razed-by-fire-in-brooklyn-thousands-of-sunday.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The structure was designed by J. Sarsfield Kennedy.<ref name="Lancaster" />

The [[Litchfield Villa]] is located near the intersection of 5th Street and Prospect Park West, directly west of the Picnic House.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The building was originally a private residence built in 1854–1857 in the [[Italianate architecture|Italianate style]]. NYC Parks has used Litchfield Villa as a maintenance and office building since the late 19th century.<ref name="Lancaster" /> The villa was listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] (NRHP) in 1977.<ref>{{NRISref|2008a|name=Litchfield Villa|refnum=77000946|access-date=January 31, 2019|dateform=mdy}}</ref> A garage compound used by NYC Parks abuts the villa directly to the south.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" />

The Tennis House, constructed in 1909–1910 by Helmle, Hudswell and Huberty, is located on the Long Meadow at West Drive, west of approximately 8th Street.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The structure is a neoclassical structure made of limestone and brick, with a red tile roof.<ref name="Tate 2015 p. 220" />{{Rp|130}} It was first used as a locker room for [[tennis]] players, but later was converted into a non-public NYC Parks facility.<ref name="Lancaster" /> By the 2000s, the structure had become dilapidated. In 2017, it was announced that the Tennis House would be renovated and converted into restrooms as part of a $5.1 million, four-year project.<ref name="BKLYNER 2017" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20170727/park-slope/prospect-park-historic-tennis-house-restoration-helmle-huberty|title=107-Year-Old Prospect Park Tennis House to Get $5.1 Million Makeover|last=Spivack|first=Caroline|date=July 27, 2017|website=DNAinfo New York|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209232042/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20170727/park-slope/prospect-park-historic-tennis-house-restoration-helmle-huberty/|archive-date=February 9, 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Roughly southeast of the Tennis House is the Dog Beach, on the western shore of the Fallkill section of the watercourse.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> It is often used by dogs and their owners during summers, since Prospect Park has an "off-leash" policy that allows unleashed dogs during early mornings and late evenings.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.timeout.com/newyork/outdoor/prospect-park-long-meadow|title=Prospect Park Long Meadow – Things to do in Prospect Park, New York|date=August 5, 2010|website=Time Out New York|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=February 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216094137/https://www.timeout.com/newyork/outdoor/prospect-park-long-meadow|url-status=live}}</ref> The beach was restored in 2017.<ref name="Peele 2017" />

[[File:Prospect Park Brooklyn Mar 2019 109.jpg|thumb|left|Bandshell]]

At 10th Street, to the west of West Drive, is the Harmony Playground and Bandshell.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The bandshell, designed by [[Aymar Embury II]], was built in 1939 on the site of a former "zoological site", which was used for archery and hockey. The bandshell and the adjacent playground were restored in 2000 and given a musical theme.<ref name="Harmony Playground : NYC Parks 1939" /> In June 2021, the Prospect Park Bandshell was renamed the Lena Horne Bandshell to honor [[Lena Horne]], a successful entertainer and Brooklyn native, as well as to show solidarity with the black community.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/news-events/news/prospect-park-bandshell-renamed-lena-horne/|title=Prospect Park Bandshell renamed Lena Horne Bandshell|publisher=prospectpark.org|date=June 25, 2021|access-date=September 1, 2021|archive-date=September 1, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210901062704/https://www.prospectpark.org/news-events/news/prospect-park-bandshell-renamed-lena-horne/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Quinn|first=Anna|title=Prospect Park Bandshell Renamed For Black Trailblazer Lena Horne|website=Park Slope, NY Patch|date=June 17, 2021|url=https://patch.com/new-york/parkslope/prospect-park-bandshell-renamed-black-trailblazer-lena-horne|access-date=August 1, 2021|archive-date=September 1, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210901120253/https://patch.com/new-york/parkslope/prospect-park-bandshell-renamed-black-trailblazer-lena-horne|url-status=live}}</ref> The bandshell hosts numerous concerts every summer through the [[Celebrate Brooklyn!|BRIC Celebrate Brooklyn!]] festival.

==== Northeast side ====
The Rose Garden is located next to Flatbush Avenue, on the north side of Prospect Park southwest of the Grand Army Plaza entrance.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> It was built on the site of the Playground, a lawn that had been the first part of Prospect Park to open.<ref name="Lancaster" /> During the late 19th and early 20th century, the garden had roses and a goldfish pond.<ref name="Scherer 2017" /> The Rose Garden was renovated in the 1960s,<ref name="Knight 1971" /> after which the garden did not host any roses.<ref name="Brooklyn Paper 2017" /><ref name="Scherer 2017" /> In 2017, the Prospect Park Alliance announced plans to restore the garden,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amny.com/news/prospect-park-rose-garden-1.18726279|title=What's in store for the Prospect Park rose garden?|last=Brown|first=Nicole|date=May 25, 2018|website=am New York|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201065655/https://www.amny.com/news/prospect-park-rose-garden-1.18726279|url-status=live}}</ref> and in the meantime, it placed 7,000 pinwheels in an effort to attract visitors.<ref name="Brooklyn Paper 2017" />

To the west, adjacent to the Rose Garden, is another garden called the Vale of Cashmere. The garden was named after [[Thomas Moore]]'s poem "Lalla Rookh",<ref name="Forgotten New York 2005"/><ref name="Scherer 2017" /> which in turn referred to [[Kashmir Valley|Kashmir]] in what was then northern India.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/01/27/archives/a-designer-of-prospect-park-stepping-out-of-olmsteds-shadow-vaux.html|title=A Designer of Prospect Park Stepping Out of Olmsted's Shadow|last=Gordon|first=David|date=January 27, 1974|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201065300/https://www.nytimes.com/1974/01/27/archives/a-designer-of-prospect-park-stepping-out-of-olmsteds-shadow-vaux.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The Vale of Cashmere was once used frequently by the well-to-do.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wnyc.org/story/vale-cashmere/|title=The Abandoned Garden of Prospect Park – New York Public Radio, Podcasts, Live Streaming Radio, News|date=August 28, 2014|website=WNYC|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201065402/https://www.wnyc.org/story/vale-cashmere/|url-status=live}}</ref> It contains a fountain that originally had a sculpture of a nude youth and six turtles in the center, though the sculpture was stolen in 1941.<ref name="Forgotten New York 2005"/> The Vale became overgrown during the 20th century, and its fountain was abandoned. The Vale of Cashmere later became a popular spot for gay [[Cruising for sex|cruising]], as documented in the book ''In the Vale of Cashmere'' by [[Thomas Roma]].<ref name="Scherer 2017" /> The woods around the vale were damaged in 2012 during Hurricane Sandy and were subsequently restored.<ref name="The New York Times 2015" />

The [[Prospect Park Zoo]] occupies a {{convert|12|acre|ha|adj=on}} plot<ref name="ppzvisitbrochure">{{Cite journal|author=Wildlife Conservation Society|date=Summer 2007|title=Prospect Park Zoo (prospectparkzoo.com) Visitor Brochure|version=200/603|publisher=Wildlife Conservation Society}}</ref> slightly south of the Rose Garden across Flatbush Avenue from [[Brooklyn Botanic Garden]].<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The zoo was opened in 1935<ref name="Lancaster" /> and has been operated by the [[Wildlife Conservation Society]] since 1980.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1980/04/23/archives/citys-3-zoos-to-be-taken-over-by-new-york-zoological-society-citys.html|title=City's 3 Zoos to Be Taken Over By New York Zoological Society; City's Zoos to Be Run by Zoological Society Zoo Was Rebuilt in 1934 $8.3 Million for Central Park|date=April 23, 1980|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201014947/https://www.nytimes.com/1980/04/23/archives/citys-3-zoos-to-be-taken-over-by-new-york-zoological-society-citys.html|url-status=live}}</ref> {{As of|2016||alt=As of 2016|df=|lc=|since=}}, Prospect Park Zoo had 864 animals representing 176 species.<ref name="AnnualReport2016">{{cite journal|author=Wildlife Conservation Society|date=December 2016|title=Annual Report 2016|url=http://www.wcs.org/media/file/annual_07.pdf|publisher=Wildlife Conservation Society|page=176 (PDF p. 81)|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080512003440/http://www.wcs.org/media/file/annual_07.pdf|archive-date=May 12, 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==== East side ====
[[File:Boathouse on the Lullwater of the Lake in Prospect Park, 3.JPG|thumb|Eastern facade of the Boathouse on the Lullwater]]
The oldest structure in Prospect Park, the [[Lefferts Historic House]], is located south of the zoo, near the intersection of Ocean Avenue, Flatbush Avenue, and Empire Boulevard.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> It was built in 1783 and was originally located near the Willink Hill entrance. The structure was relocated in 1920 to make way for the Willink entrance.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/facilities/historichouses|title=Prospect Park Historic Houses : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201013553/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/facilities/historichouses|url-status=live}}</ref> The house is a [[List of New York City Designated Landmarks in Brooklyn|New York City designated landmark]] and operates as a children's museum of Brooklyn family life during the 19th century.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/09/16/arts/another-star-vehicle-has-its-revival.html|title=Another Star Vehicle Has Its Revival|last=Graeber|first=Laurel|date=September 16, 2005|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201013326/https://www.nytimes.com/2005/09/16/arts/another-star-vehicle-has-its-revival.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The Prospect Park Carousel is located immediately west of the Lefferts Historic House.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The carousel contains 53 horses, created by master horse carver [[Charles Carmel]] in 1912, as well as three carvings of other animals and two chariots.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/visit-the-park/places-to-go/carousel/|title=Carousel in Prospect Park|website=Prospect Park|access-date=February 15, 2019|archive-date=March 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190316021419/https://www.prospectpark.org/visit-the-park/places-to-go/carousel/|url-status=live}}</ref> The carousel opened in October 1952,<ref name="Hanmer 1952" /><ref name="The New York Times 1952" /> superseding another carousel that had burned down over twenty years earlier.<ref name="BDE-Carousels-1952">{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/55322531|title=Carousel Promised for Prospect Park|date=April 15, 1952|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=February 14, 2019|page=8|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=February 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216035402/http://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/55322531/|url-status=live}}</ref> It was subsequently restored from 1971 to 1974,<ref name="Cadkin 1974" /> and again from 1987 to 1989.<ref name="Martin 1989" /> Prior to the opening of the current carousel, three separate wooden carousels had been built throughout the park's history, and were located in different parts of the park.<ref name="Lancaster" />

The Willink Hill entrance contains the neoclassical Willink Entrance Comfort Station.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The structure opened in 1912 and is designed similarly to the Tennis House.<ref name="Tate 2015 p. 220" />{{Rp|130}}<ref name="Lancaster" />

Further south of the Willink entrance is the [[Boathouse on the Lullwater of the Lake in Prospect Park|Boathouse on the Lullwater]], on the Lullwater's eastern shore.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> Built in 1905–1907, it was the first structure in the park built by McKim, Mead and White, and was also constructed in the neoclassical style.<ref name="Tate 2015 p. 220" />{{Rp|130}} After being saved from destruction in 1964,<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Scherer 2017">{{cite web|url=https://ny.curbed.com/maps/prospect-park-brooklyn-things-to-do|title=15 hidden gems of Prospect Park|last=Scherer|first=Jenna|date=August 10, 2017|website=Curbed NY|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201065235/https://ny.curbed.com/maps/prospect-park-brooklyn-things-to-do|url-status=dead}}</ref> it was listed on the NRHP in 1972.<ref>{{NRISref|2008a|name=Boathouse on the Lullwater of the Lake in Prospect Park|refnum=72000850|access-date=January 31, 2019|dateform=mdy}}</ref>

[[File:Prospect Park Oriental Pavilion Golden Hour 2.jpg|left|thumb|A path leading to the Oriental Pavilion]]

South of the Boathouse, past the Cleft Ridge Arch, is the [[Concert Grove]], located on the northeast edge of the Lake.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> Originally built in 1847,<ref name="NYCgo.com">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgo.com/arts-culture/prospect-park-concert-grove|title=Prospect Park Concert Grove|website=NYCgo.com|access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201070846/https://www.nycgo.com/arts-culture/prospect-park-concert-grove|url-status=live}}</ref> it was designed so park patrons could hear music being played on the later-demolished Music Island. The grove's style complements that of the [[Central Park Mall]] but was laid out radially.<ref name="Lancaster" /> The grove also contains busts of classical composers.<ref name="Scherer 2017" /> A statue of Abraham Lincoln is located at the Concert Grove.<ref name="NYCParksLincoln"/> In the middle of the grove is the Concert Grove Pavilion, also known as the Oriental Pavilion, measuring {{Convert|40|by|80|ft|m|abbr=}} with a roof and columns in a Middle Eastern or Indian style;<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Scherer 2017" /> it formerly served as a restaurant but has since fallen into disrepair.<ref name="The New York Times 2015" /><ref name="NYCgo.com" /> In 2021, the Concert Grove Pavilion was restored.<ref name="Rahmanan 2021">{{cite web|last=Rahmanan|first=Anna|title=The concert pavilion in Prospect Park has reopened after seven years|website=Time Out New York|date=April 9, 2021|url=https://www.timeout.com/newyork/news/the-concert-pavilion-in-prospect-park-has-reopened-after-seven-years-040921|access-date=August 1, 2021|archive-date=September 1, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210901120252/https://www.timeout.com/newyork/news/the-concert-pavilion-in-prospect-park-has-reopened-after-seven-years-040921|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Verde 2021">{{cite web|last=Verde|first=Ben|title=Restored Concert Grove Pavilion in Prospect Park reopens after six-year closure|website=Brooklyn Paper|date=April 7, 2021|url=https://www.brooklynpaper.com/concert-grove-pavilion-reopens-prospect-park-april-2021/|access-date=August 1, 2021|archive-date=June 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210616231725/https://www.brooklynpaper.com/concert-grove-pavilion-reopens-prospect-park-april-2021/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The Samuel J. and Ethel LeFrak Center at Lakeside is located immediately south of the Concert Grove.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> It was completed in December 2013 and replaces the former Wollman Rink.<ref name="NYC.gov-Lakeside-2013"/><ref name="NYTimes-Lakeside-2013"/> The multipurpose, year-round facility is used for ice-skating, boating, biking, and roller-skating, as well as winter sports such as [[ice hockey|hockey]] and [[curling]].<ref name="NYTimes-EnjoyPP-2018"/><ref name="PP-LeFrak"/> The LeFrak Center accommodates over 200,000 visitors annually.<ref name="Lakeside" />

==== Nethermead and Lookout Hill ====
[[File:Music Pagoda in Prospect Park (81543p).jpg|thumb|Rebuilt Music Pagoda]]

The Music Pagoda is located in the Nethermead, on the east side of the park along the watercourse's west shore.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> The original pagoda, built in 1887, was a wooden structure with an octagonal roof and a stone base. It replaced a "temporary" music stand near the Lullwood.<ref name="Lancaster" /> The Music Pagoda was used for concerts until it burned down in 1968. The current pagoda on the site is a re-creation of the original, built in 1971.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://forgotten-ny.com/2015/10/music-pagoda-prospect-park-2/|title=MUSIC PAGODA, Prospect Park|date=October 30, 2015|website=Forgotten New York|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209180246/https://forgotten-ny.com/2015/10/music-pagoda-prospect-park-2/|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{Anchor|Well House}}The Well House is located on the northern shore of the Lake, abutting the southern slope of Lookout Hill on the southwestern side of Prospect Park.<ref name="Forgotten New York 2005" /><ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> It was the last structure in the park to be built by Olmsted and Vaux, having been built in 1869. It was made of gray stone and brick, and featured a [[hip roof]] and a doorway inside a [[Four-centred arch|Tudor arch]]. The house initially contained machinery that powered Prospect Park's watercourse, and at one point, pumped {{Convert|750,000|gal|L|sp=us|abbr=off}} of water into the watercourse each day.<ref name="Lancaster" /> The water from the Well House was drawn from a {{Convert|70|ft|m|-deep|abbr=|adj=mid}} [[well]], which led to the Brooklyn Aquifer.<ref name="Kadinsky20162" /><ref name="Brooklyn Paper 2011" /> Originally, there was a {{Convert|60|ft|m|-tall|abbr=|adj=mid}} smokestack behind the Well House, as well as a [[cistern]] in front of the building.<ref name="Kadinsky20162" /><ref name="Vries 2018" /> The machines became obsolete in the early 20th century when Prospect Park was connected to [[New York City water supply system|New York City's municipal water system]].<ref name="Warerkar 2017" /><ref name="Vries 2018" />  Subsequently, the tower was demolished and the cistern was filled in.<ref name="Vries 2018" /> In 2017, the Well House was restored and turned into a composting restroom.<ref name="Spectrum News NY1 {{pipe}} New York City 2017" /><ref name="Warerkar 2017" />

==== South side ====
[[File:The Peristyle.JPG|thumb|The Peristyle]]
The [[Grecian Shelter|Prospect Park Peristyle]], also known as the Grecian Shelter or Croquet Shelter, is located on the southwest corner of the park, south of the Lake.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /> Constructed by McKim, Mead and White in 1905, this [[peristyle]] was built on the site of the 1860s-era Promenade Drive Shelter. The Prospect Park Peristyle is actually designed in the [[Renaissance architecture|Renaissance architectural style]] and consists of a rectangular [[colonnade]] with [[Corinthian order|Corinthian columns]].<ref name="Lancaster" /> It was rehabilitated in 1966 and listed on the NRHP in 1972.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.brownstoner.com/brooklyn-life/building-of-the-day-prospect-park-peristyle/|title=Building of the Day: Prospect Park Peristyle|last=Spellen|first=Suzanne|date=May 1, 2012|website=Brownstoner|access-date=February 2, 2019|archive-date=February 2, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190202095434/https://www.brownstoner.com/brooklyn-life/building-of-the-day-prospect-park-peristyle/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Former structures ===
[[File:DairyFarmhouseProspectParkBrooklyn.jpg|thumb|The Dairy, {{Circa}} 1870|alt=The Dairy Cottage, seen circa 1870]]
The Dairy Cottage, or "the Dairy", was located near Boulder Bridge west of the zoo. It was a two-story stone [[cottage]] with two [[gable]]d wings; a public room and women's quarters on the first floor; and a single residence on the second floor.<ref name="Lancaster" /> The Dairy was built in 1869 or 1871 to sell fresh [[milk]] and other light refreshments to the public; [[the Dairy|a similar building]] was also built in Central Park. At the time, [[sheep]] and [[Cattle|cows]] were allowed to pasture on the meadows of Prospect Park, and seven cows were purchased specifically to provide milk. However, according to the ''Brooklyn Daily Eagle'', news articles after 1879 do not make a mention of the Dairy providing milk.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/27868005/|title=Park Once Operated Own Dairy Business|date=May 1, 1932|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=January 31, 2019|page=16|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041810/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/article/the-brooklyn-daily-eagle-park-once-opera/27868005/|url-status=live}}</ref> The cottage later became part of the Menagerie, the precursor to the modern-day zoo, and was encircled by several other zoo buildings to its north and east. All of these buildings were demolished in 1935 when the zoo was built.<ref name="Lancaster" />

There were two unusual structures built in Prospect Park in its early years. The first was a [[camera obscura]] booth located on Breeze Hill's western slope, at the east end of the park, built in the early 1880s.<ref name="am New York 2014" /><ref name="Forgotten New York 2005" /> The second was the Circular Yacht or Rotary Yacht, a floating [[carousel]] with yacht-shaped vehicles. Located near the Long Meadow, the Circular Yacht was constructed by inventor David Smith in 1878 and could hold up to 220 people at once.<ref name="am New York 2014" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/news-events/news/prospect-parks-bizarre-rotary-yacht/|title=Prospect Park's Bizarre Bygone Attraction|date=October 17, 2018|website=Prospect Park|access-date=February 7, 2019|archive-date=February 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209124301/https://www.prospectpark.org/news-events/news/prospect-parks-bizarre-rotary-yacht/|url-status=live}}</ref> These structures were both demolished before the 1900s, and the camera obscura later became the site of the now-demolished Old Fashioned Flower Garden.<ref name="am New York 2014" /><ref name="Lancaster" />

The park contained a Music Island near the east shore of the Lake.<ref name="Lancaster" /> The island was used by musicians who were performing for audiences in the nearby Concert Grove. It was demolished in 1960 to make way for the Wollman Rink. Following the rink's demolition in the early 2010s,<ref name="Pollak 2011" /> a replica of the island was constructed, and it opened in 2012.<ref name="Dunlap 2012" /><ref name="New York City Department of Parks & Recreation 2012" /> Across the Lake, two structures were built on the peninsula in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The Model Yacht Club House, built on the south side of the peninsula in 1900, was an octagonal wood-frame clubhouse that burned down in a fire in 1956. On the opposite or northern side of the peninsula, there was another shelter, similar in design to the Concert Grove Pavilion, which lasted from 1915 to around the 1940s.<ref name="Lancaster" /><ref name="Forgotten New York 2005" />

On the west side of Prospect Park, there was a conservatory on the Long Meadow. It consisted of sixteen greenhouses located near Seventh Street and Prospect Park West.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28451051/|title=Prospect Park to Get Only Flower Shows|date=January 3, 1939|work=New York Daily News|access-date=February 14, 2019|page=275|via=Newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041709/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-prospect-park-to-get-only-flo/28451051/|url-status=live}}</ref> Though it was a popular visitor attraction, it was supplanted by the [[Brooklyn Botanic Garden]] past the park's eastern edge. The conservatory's greenhouses were renovated in 1929–1930, but the cost of upkeep soon became exorbitant.<ref name="Lancaster" /> In 1955, the greenhouses were considered redundant and were demolished. At that point, the conservatory's main attraction was an annual Easter flower show.<ref name="Green">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1955/03/23/archives/city-to-discard-17-greenhouses-75yearold-structures-in-prospect.html|title=City to Discard 17 Greenhouses|date=May 23, 1955|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=August 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190821003141/https://www.nytimes.com/1955/03/23/archives/city-to-discard-17-greenhouses-75yearold-structures-in-prospect.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28451146/|title=Cashmore OKd End of Greenhouses|first=David|last=Gordon|date=March 24, 1955|work=New York Daily News|access-date=February 14, 2019|page=97|via=Newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041710/https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-cashmore-okd-end-of-greenhous/28451146/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Parade Ground ===
<!-- Note: [[Flatbush, Brooklyn]] links to this section-->The site of the present-day Parade Ground, at Prospect Park's southwest corner, was first proposed in 1866 and was to be used for training militia.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/50391815/|title=Our Albany Correspondence; An Important Question to Tax-payers|date=March 14, 1866|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=February 12, 2019|page=2|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=February 13, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190213011050/https://www.newspapers.com/image/50391815/|url-status=live}}</ref> The state approved the acquisition of a {{Convert|40|acre|0|abbr=|adj=on}} rectangular area just south of Parkside Avenue and handed control of the plot to the Prospect Park commissioners.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dstDAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA236|title=Annual Reports of the Brooklyn Park Commissioners, 1861–1873: Reprinted by Order of the Board, with Such Acts of the Legislature in Their Amended Form, as Relate to the Brooklyn Parks, and Their Management|last=Brooklyn (New York, N. Y. ) Park Commissioners|date=1873|pages=236|language=en|access-date=February 12, 2019|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041807/https://books.google.com/books?id=dstDAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA236#v=onepage&q&f=false|url-status=live}}</ref> The Parade Ground was designated to be used for sports and military drills. It was set apart from the main section of the park in fear that the high level of activity would damage the grass and plants and disrupt the park's pastoral feel. Initially, the Parade Ground contained a long, wood-frame building, which included a two-story pavilion for officers' quarters, as well as a restroom to the south and a guard room to the north.<ref name="Lancaster" /> Other uses included a gathering on June 15, 1927, when the Parade Ground attracted over 200,000 people to greet pioneering aviator [[Charles Lindbergh]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/59851774/|title=Huge Brooklyn Crowds Hail Lindbergh|date=June 6, 1927|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=August 28, 2019|page=1|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=August 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190829010408/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/59851774/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://forgotten-ny.com/2018/06/parade-ground-flatbush/|title=PARADE GROUND, Flatbush|last=Walsh|first=Kevin|date=June 13, 2018|website=Forgotten New York|language=en-US|access-date=August 29, 2019|archive-date=August 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190829003448/https://forgotten-ny.com/2018/06/parade-ground-flatbush/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The militia no longer use the Parade Ground, but the plot is still an active athletic complex.<ref name="New York City Department of Parks & Recreation 1939">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/parade-ground/history|title=Parade Ground Highlights : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=January 28, 2019|archive-date=January 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129064140/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/parade-ground/history|url-status=live}}</ref> In its present form, the Parade Ground has fifteen numbered courts and fields, used for soccer, baseball, softball, basketball, and volleyball.<ref name="Prospect Park Alliance 2018" /><ref name="New York City Department of Parks & Recreation 1939" /> They encompass the Prospect Park Tennis Center, four baseball diamonds, two softball fields, a football field, a soccer field, basketball and volleyball courts, the Paul Ricard [[Pétanque]] Court and three giant multi-use fields.<ref name="New York City Department of Parks & Recreation 1939" /> The Stewart Playground is also on the east side of the Parade Ground.<ref>{{cite web|title=Detective Dillon Stewart Playground : NYC Parks|website=Prospect Park Highlights|date=June 26, 1939|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/highlights/19704|access-date=March 11, 2021|archive-date=March 5, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210305225658/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B073/highlights/19704|url-status=live}}</ref>

Many Major League Baseball stars got their start at the Parade Ground, including Joe Torre and [[Sandy Koufax]].<ref name="New York City Department of Parks & Recreation 1939" /> In 2003, the Parade Ground had a [[netball]] court installed next to the basketball courts.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.brooklynhistory.org/wp-content/uploads/BBNH_CaseStudyFolders.pdf|title=Prospect Park: A Place to Play|work=Bats, Balls, Nets & Hoops: Stories of Sports in Brooklyn|publisher=Brooklyn Public Library|access-date=October 21, 2019|archive-date=March 8, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308173348/https://www.brooklynhistory.org/wp-content/uploads/BBNH_CaseStudyFolders.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> The next year, the Parade Ground underwent a $12.4 million restoration.<ref name="New York City Department of Parks & Recreation 1939" /> The netball court was replaced by an outdoor adult fitness center in 2019, due to a lack of use,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bklyner.com/new-adult-fitness-area-opens-in-prospect-park/|title=New Adult Fitness Area Opens In Prospect Park|last=Wong|first=Pamela|date=May 6, 2019|website=BKLYNER|language=en-US|access-date=October 21, 2019|archive-date=May 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190509063945/https://bklyner.com/new-adult-fitness-area-opens-in-prospect-park/|url-status=live}}</ref> and a dog run in the Parade Ground opened in 2020.<ref name=bhr20200707/>

== Management ==
A [[nonprofit organization]] called Prospect Park Alliance manages Prospect Park, while NYC Parks owns and operates the land and facilities. The Alliance's responsibilities include maintaining and restoring natural and recreational areas, as well as providing educational and cultural programs.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/learn-more/what-we-do/|title=About the Alliance|date=January 22, 2019|website=Prospect Park|access-date=February 16, 2019|archive-date=February 17, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190217084925/https://www.prospectpark.org/learn-more/what-we-do/|url-status=live}}</ref> In the fiscal year ending June 30, 2022, the Alliance had [[Net worth|net assets]] ([[Equity (finance)|own equity]]) of about $37.2 million and [[Liability (financial accounting)|liabilities]] of $3.1 million, which amounted to total [[asset]]s of $40.3 million. Net assets increased $5.9 million from the fiscal year ending June 30, 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.prospectpark.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/FY22-Audited-Financial-Statements.pdf|title=Financial Statement for the Year Ending June 30, 2022|date=June 30, 2022|website=Prospect Park Alliance|pages=4–5|access-date=February 16, 2023|archive-date=March 12, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230312033518/https://www.prospectpark.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/FY22-Audited-Financial-Statements.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

Prior to the Prospect Park Alliance's founding, there was no private maintenance of the park. The Alliance was created in April 1987<ref name="NYTimes-PPA-Creation-1987" /> after the city had spent $10 million in federal funds to renovate the park in the early 1980s.<ref name="Laskow 2014" /> The Alliance subsequently started new programs to reach out to the surrounding communities, and its renovation programs caused housing prices in the area to increase by the 1990s.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/05/01/nyregion/a-critical-tour-of-the-empire-battery-park-to-high-bridge.html|title=A Critical Tour of the Empire: Battery Park to High Bridge|date=May 1, 1994|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=October 11, 2017|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=September 28, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170928104808/http://www.nytimes.com/1994/05/01/nyregion/a-critical-tour-of-the-empire-battery-park-to-high-bridge.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Transportation ==
[[File:Prospect Park entrance 4 vc.jpg|thumb|Entrance to the [[Prospect Park (BMT Brighton Line)|Prospect Park]] station]]

There are four [[New York City Subway]] stations that directly serve the park.<ref>{{NYCS const|map}}</ref> The eastern side of Prospect Park is served by [[Prospect Park (BMT Brighton Line)|the park's eponymous station]] ({{NYCS trains|Prospect Park}}) and the [[Parkside Avenue (BMT Brighton Line)|Parkside Avenue]] station ({{NYCS trains|Brighton local|time=nolink}}). The western side is served by [[15th Street–Prospect Park (IND Culver Line)|15th Street–Prospect Park]] ({{NYCS trains|Culver IND north}}). Grand Army Plaza is served by the {{NYCS trains|Eastern west local header}} at [[Grand Army Plaza (IRT Eastern Parkway Line)|the plaza's eponymous station]].<ref name="Metropolitan Transportation Authority 2018">{{Cite NYCS map|neighborhood|Park Slope}}</ref> Bus service is provided on the western side by the {{NYC bus link|B61|B67|B69|prose=y}} buses, the southwestern side by the {{NYC bus link|B68}} bus; the eastern side by the {{NYC bus link|B16|B41|B43|B48|prose=y}} buses; and the southern side by the B16 bus.<ref name="Metropolitan Transportation Authority 2018" /><ref>{{Cite NYC bus map|B}}</ref>

==Incidents==
===Animals===
During the 1970s, there were multiple incidents involving animal injuries or deaths at the Prospect Park Zoo. This included the scalding death of a monkey in 1975, allegedly by a zoo employee, as well as an acting zoo director who was accused of shooting at pigeons and killing zoo animals.<ref>{{cite news|title=The Zoo Story: Part Two|first=Roger|last=Parloff|work=New York Magazine|publisher=New York Media, LLC|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ctECAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA62|date=May 7, 1979|language=en|access-date=February 20, 2019|page=62|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041708/https://books.google.com/books?id=ctECAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA62#v=onepage&q&f=false|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Fowler 1976"/> A zoo employee also locked himself in a monkey enclosure for several hours in 1974 to protest the deaths of ten animals.<ref name="Fowler 1976"/><ref>{{cite news|title=It's A Jungle in Here|first=Tad|last=Friend|date=April 24, 1995|work=New York Magazine|publisher=New York Media, LLC|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C-UCAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA48|language=en|access-date=February 20, 2019|page=48|archive-date=January 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240124041811/https://books.google.com/books?id=C-UCAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA48#v=onepage&q&f=false|url-status=live}}</ref> These incidents, as well as several others at the [[Central Park Zoo]], prompted protests by animal-rights groups who wanted to close the two zoos and move the animals to the larger [[Bronx Zoo]].<ref name="Fowler 1976">{{cite web|last=Fowler|first=Glenn|title=Prospect Park Zoo Head Accused of Killing Animals|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|date=April 1, 1976|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1976/05/01/archives/prospect-park-zoo-head-accused-of-killing-animals.html|access-date=February 20, 2019|archive-date=February 21, to the Wildlife Conservation Society's takeover of the Prospect Park Zoo in 1980.<ref name="NYZooTakeOver"/>

In May 1987, an 11-year-old boy climbed into the [[polar bear]] enclosure after hours at the Prospect Park Zoo and was subsequently mauled by two of the bears; both bears were then fatally shot by police officers. The incident contributed to the Wildlife Conservation Society's decision to redesign the zoo to emphasize species more appropriate to its small size and to visitor interactions.<ref>{{cite news|title=Polar Bears Kill a Child at the Prospect Park Zoo|first=James|last=Barron|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/05/20/nyregion/polar-bears-kill-a-child-at-prospect-park-zoo.html|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=May 20, 1987|access-date=January 25, 2011|archive-date=April 29, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110429224044/http://www.nytimes.com/1987/05/20/nyregion/polar-bears-kill-a-child-at-prospect-park-zoo.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

In July 2010, federal authorities captured 400 [[Canada geese]] in the park and gassed them to death due to [[air safety]] concerns brought up after the emergency landing of [[US Airways Flight 1549]] in January 2009.<ref>{{cite news|title=400 Park Geese Die, for Human Fliers' Sake|first=Isolde|last=Raftery|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/07/13/nyregion/13geese.html|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|date=July 12, 2010|access-date=January 25, 2011|archive-date=April 29, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110429224102/http://www.nytimes.com/2010/07/13/nyregion/13geese.html|url-status=live}}</ref>
